lessons.title: Amplitude, period and wavelength
lessons.summary: Distinguish wave size, repetition time and wavelength, and predict how they change.
lessons.body:
Every sound your synth makes ends up as a speaker cone pushing air back and forth. The air pressure at your ear rises and falls around normal atmospheric pressure, and your ear turns that pattern into what you hear.

Inside the synth there is no air. There is first a sequence of numbers, then a voltage on a wire. The vocabulary is the same at every stage, though. Here, a *waveform* describes how a quantity (pressure, voltage, or a number in memory) changes over time, and we describe it by how big the change is, how often it repeats and where in its cycle it is.

Start by distinguishing how large a wave is, how often it repeats and how far it travels.

## The four basic measurements

Picture one repeating cycle of a wave plotted against time:

```diagram
 +A |    .-'''-.
    |  .'       '.
  0 +-'-----------'.-----------.-> t
    |               '.       .'
 -A |                 '-...-'
    |<------- one period T ----->|
```

- **Amplitude (A)** is how far the wave swings from its centre line. In air that's a pressure difference; in a circuit it's volts; in software it's a number, conventionally between −1 and +1. Bigger amplitude sounds louder, though loudness perception is more complicated than amplitude alone.
- **Period (T)** is the time one full cycle takes, in seconds.
- **Frequency (f)** is how many cycles happen per second, in hertz (Hz). It's the reciprocal of the period (one divided by the period).
- **Wavelength** (λ) is the *distance* one cycle covers as it travels through a medium such as air.

Frequency and period are two views of the same thing: if you know how long one cycle takes, you know how many fit in a second.

For scale, a 440 Hz wave completes each cycle in about 2.27 milliseconds (ms). The relationship is exact for any repeating wave; it only stops being meaningful for sounds that don't repeat, such as noise.

Wavelength needs one more ingredient, the speed at which the wave travels. In the time of one period, the wave moves forward by one wavelength:

```formula reference
λ = c / f
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength: the distance one cycle occupies as it travels, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in the medium, in metres per second (m/s); about 343 m/s in dry air at 20 °C
f: the frequency of the wave, in hertz (Hz)
m: metres
m/s: metres per second
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: the wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency, so higher notes have shorter wavelengths. A 440 Hz tone in air has a wavelength of about 0.78 m.
```

The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature (it is faster in warmer air and much faster in water or steel), so wavelength depends on the conditions in which sound travels.

Wavelength matters for room acoustics and speaker design, including room resonances and how sound diffracts around obstacles. Inside a synth it barely matters at all: your signals live as samples and voltages, where only time and frequency count. Don't confuse *wavelength* with *period*. One is metres, the other seconds.

Human hearing is usually quoted as roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20,000 Hz). The top end falls with age, and that range is a rule of thumb rather than a hard limit. In air, those frequencies have wavelengths of roughly 17 m down to 1.7 cm.

## Key takeaways

- Amplitude measures the size of the swing; frequency measures cycles per second.
- Frequency and period are reciprocals: doubling one halves the other.
- Wavelength is a distance in a medium; period is a time. Inside a synth, work with time and frequency.

## Further reading

- [Sine wave — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)
- [Speed of sound — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_sound)
- [Sound speed, frequency and wavelength — OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/17-2-speed-of-sound-frequency-and-wavelength)

lessons.title: Phase and radians
lessons.summary: Measure position within a cycle and explain reinforcement, cancellation and phase jumps.
lessons.body:
## Phase and radians

The **phase of a wave** says *where in its cycle* it is at a given moment. You can measure it in fractions of a cycle (0 to 1), degrees (0° to 360°), or **radians** (0 to 2π). Maths libraries use radians, so get comfortable with them.

A radian measures an angle by comparing arc length with circle radius. One full turn is about 6.283 radians. Cycle fractions, degrees and radians are three units for the same position:

| Cycles | Degrees | Radians |
|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 90° | π/2 ≈ 1.571 |
| 0.5 | 180° | π ≈ 3.142 |
| 1 | 360° | 2π ≈ 6.283 |

Phase matters most when you **combine** waves. Two identical sines in phase add up to double the amplitude. Shift one by half a cycle (π radians, 180°) and they cancel completely. Anywhere in between gives partial reinforcement or partial cancellation. That's why detuned oscillators "beat", and why some layered sounds go thin when a phase relationship shifts.

Phase on its own, for a single steady tone, is mostly inaudible. Your ear can't tell a sine from the same sine starting a quarter-cycle later. What you *can* hear is a sudden phase **jump** in the middle of a tone: the waveform can jump to a new value instantly, creating a click. A phase change at a specially chosen point can leave the value unchanged, so a click is not inevitable.

## Pitfalls

- **Degrees passed to `sin`.** If phase is in degrees, convert it with `math.radians` before calling `math.sin`. A quarter-cycle should reach the positive peak, rather than an arbitrary value.

## Key takeaways

- One full cycle is 2π radians; maths-library sine functions expect radians.
- Relative phase controls how two waves reinforce or cancel.
- A sudden phase change can create a discontinuity and a click.

## Further reading

- [Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html)
- [Phase (waves) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_(waves))

options.text: Limit the phase to 90 degrees
options.explanation: The range is not the problem; sine repeats for any real angle.

options.text: Convert degrees to radians before calling `math.sin`
options.explanation: Correct. Python’s sine function expects radians, so the phase unit must match its interface.

options.text: Multiply the output by 360
options.explanation: Output gain cannot correct an input angle unit mismatch.

options.explanation: Bit depth does not change the unit expected by the sine function.

questions.prompt: Which statements about phase are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adding two identical sines that are 180° (π radians) out of phase gives silence
options.explanation: Correct. At every instant one is the negative of the other, so the sum is zero.

options.text: A sudden jump in an oscillator's phase partway through a note is usually heard as a click
options.explanation: Correct. A phase jump generally makes the waveform value change abruptly between two samples, and that step contains energy at many frequencies.

options.text: A steady sine started a quarter-cycle late sounds clearly different from one started on time
options.explanation: A constant phase offset on a single steady tone is essentially inaudible. Phase matters when signals are combined or when it changes abruptly.

options.text: Phase is measured in hertz
options.explanation: Hertz is cycles per second, a unit of frequency. Phase is a position in the cycle: radians, degrees or fractions of a cycle.

options.text: π/2 radians is the same phase as 90°
options.explanation: Correct. A full cycle is 2π radians or 360°, so a quarter of a cycle, π/2 radians, is 90°.

questions.workedExample: Identical equal-level sines half a cycle apart cancel sample by sample. A sudden phase change can instead jump the waveform value and click; specially timed changes may avoid that step. A fixed starting offset on a lone steady sine is essentially inaudible. Phase is position in a cycle, so use angles or cycle fractions, rather than hertz. A quarter-turn is 90 degrees or pi over two radians.

lessons.title: Build a sine from its parameters
lessons.summary: Explain how frequency, elapsed time, phase and amplitude determine a sine’s value.
lessons.body:
## The sine wave formula

The purest tone is a sine wave. This formula gives its value at any moment, and it is the starting point for every oscillator in the project:

```formula essential
x(t) = A × sin(2 × π × f × t + φ)
where
x(t): the value of the wave at time t: a pressure, a voltage or a sample value, depending on where the wave lives
t: the time since the wave started, in seconds (s)
A: the amplitude, the largest value the wave reaches; in software usually at most 1.0
sin: the sine function, which turns an angle in radians into a value that swings smoothly between −1 and +1 and repeats every 2π
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second
φ: phi, the starting phase, in radians (rad): where in the cycle the wave is at t = 0
In words: To generate a sine, advance through cycles at the desired frequency, convert to radians, add the starting phase, take the sine and scale by amplitude.
```

Read it from the inside out:

1. **f·t** is the number of cycles completed after t seconds. At 440 Hz, after 0.01 s you've done 4.4 cycles.
2. **2π·f·t** converts cycles to radians, because `sin` wants radians.
3. **φ** (phi) is the starting phase, in radians. A starting phase of π/2 turns a sine into a cosine.
4. **A** scales the result, which otherwise swings between −1 and +1.

For a sine starting at zero, a quarter-cycle reaches the positive peak, a half-cycle returns to zero and three quarters reaches the negative peak. An amplitude of 0.5 makes those peaks +0.5 and −0.5, whatever the frequency. Frequency determines how quickly you reach them.

The formula describes an ideal, never-ending tone; real notes start, stop and change, which is what the rest of the module deals with.

Frequency can also be measured in radians per second, called **angular frequency**. One cycle contains two pi radians, so angular frequency is about 6.283 times the cycles-per-second value.

> [!note] Why the sine is special
> A sine contains exactly one frequency. An ideal periodic waveform (a sawtooth, a square, or a repeating approximation to a sustained violin tone) can be built by adding sines at whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency. Those whole-number components are its **harmonics**, and their amplitude recipe is a big part of its **timbre**. A real recorded note also changes over time and can contain noise. The synthesis module builds on this.

## Pitfalls

- **Forgetting the 2π.** `sin(f·t)` produces a tone 2π times too low (440 Hz becomes about 70 Hz).

## Key takeaways

- Frequency and elapsed time determine the number of cycles completed.
- Convert cycles to radians, add starting phase, then take the sine and scale its amplitude.
- Angular frequency measures radians per second; harmonics build richer periodic waveforms.

## Further reading

- [Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html)
- [Sine wave — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)
- [Python sine and angle functions — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html)

questions.prompt: A sine has amplitude 0.5, starts at phase zero and is evaluated one quarter of a cycle after it starts. What is its value?

options.explanation: Zero is the value at the start or half-cycle point; a quarter-cycle is the positive peak.
The sine function reaches 1, but the amplitude multiplier halves that value.
Correct. A quarter-cycle is π/2 radians, where sine is 1; multiplying by amplitude 0.5 gives 0.5.
The negative peak occurs at three quarters of a cycle, not one quarter.

questions.workedExample: Starting at zero phase, the sine rises to its positive peak after a quarter-cycle. Amplitude sets that peak, so it is +0.5. Frequency changes how long the quarter-cycle takes, rather than changing the peak value.

lessons.title: Samples per cycle and phase increment
lessons.summary: Predict how pitch and sample rate change samples per cycle and per-sample phase advance.
lessons.body:
## From time to samples

A digital synth computes values only at evenly spaced sample instants. The **sample rate** says how many of these occur each second; 48,000 per second is a common rate.

Each sample uses the sine’s value at that instant. The first sample is at the start, the next is one sample period later, and so on; samples need not land on peaks or whole-cycle boundaries.

Two practical quantities describe how an oscillator moves through those instants.

**Samples per period** tells you how many numbers describe one cycle:

```formula reference
S = fs / f
where
S: the number of samples in one cycle (samples per period); not usually a whole number
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second; here 440
In words: divide samples per second by cycles per second to get samples per cycle. A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz spans about 109 samples.
```

**Phase increment** is how far round the cycle you move between one sample and the next. It's the reciprocal of samples per period:

```formula reference
Δp = f / fs
Δθ = 2πΔp
where
Δp: delta p, the phase increment in cycles per sample (the Greek letter Δ, delta, means "a step in")
Δθ: delta theta, the same increment measured in radians per sample
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second
π: pi, about 3.14159
cycles: fractions of one full cycle
rad: radians; one full cycle is 2π radians
In words: Higher frequency advances phase further at each sample; a higher sample rate needs smaller steps for the same pitch. Convert a cycle step to radians by multiplying by two pi.
```

At 48 kHz, a 440 Hz cycle spans about 109 sample periods, while a 3520 Hz cycle spans fewer than 14. Those spans need not be whole numbers.

Notice:

- Samples per period is rarely a whole number. A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz takes 109.09 samples, so the samples land at slightly different points of each cycle. That's fine; the phase is tracked as a real number.
- Higher pitches get **fewer** samples per cycle. At 3520 Hz you have under 14 points per cycle. The Nyquist-limit unit shows where this runs out.
- The phase increment depends on **both** tone frequency and sample rate. Change the rate to 44.1 kHz and the step for every note changes. If a synth assumes the wrong sample rate, every note comes out at the wrong pitch.

## Pitfalls

- **Hard-coding the sample rate.** Compute the increment from the actual rate the audio hardware is running at.

## Key takeaways

- Sample time is the sample index divided by the sample rate.
- Samples per period is sample rate divided by tone frequency; it need not be a whole number.
- Phase increment is tone frequency divided by sample rate in cycles per sample. Use the hardware’s actual rate.

## Further reading

- [Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html)
- [Numerically controlled oscillator (phase accumulator) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerically_controlled_oscillator)

options.text: It plays flat by the same frequency ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Each sample advances the assumed step, but fewer steps occur per second.

options.text: It stays in tune because the note frequency is in the code
options.explanation: The code chooses progress per sample; the clock determines samples per second.

questions.prompt: A sound’s wavelength changes when it enters a medium where sound travels faster, while its frequency stays the same. Must the synth change the samples that generated the tone?

options.text: Yes: it needs a longer memory buffer for the longer wavelength
options.explanation: Wavelength is distance in the medium, not audio buffer length.

options.text: No: wavelength describes propagation; oscillator samples depend on timing, amplitude and phase
options.explanation: Correct. The medium changes the distance between wave cycles, not the digital cycle timing.

options.text: Yes: the sample rate must equal the speed of sound
options.explanation: Sample rate measures samples per second; sound speed measures distance per second.

options.text: No: wavelength and frequency are always independent
options.explanation: At a given propagation speed they are linked; the medium’s speed also matters.

questions.workedExample: Separate the digital time sequence from the sound travelling in a medium. A faster propagation speed increases wavelength for a fixed frequency. No distance measurement is needed to generate the same oscillator samples.

lessons.title: Keep a wrapped phase accumulator
lessons.summary: Preserve phase through frequency changes and processing blocks without an ever-growing counter.
lessons.body:
## The phase accumulator

A sine can be evaluated using each sample’s elapsed time. Many real oscillators instead keep the **phase of a wave** in a running variable and add the increment each sample, wrapping it back into range after each full cycle:

```python
import math

fs, f = 48_000, 440.0
inc = f / fs
phase = 0.0          # cycles, in [0, 1)
out = []
for n in range(6):
    # Read the wave at the current phase.
    out.append(math.sin(2*math.pi*phase))
    phase += inc
    # Wrap after one full cycle.
    if phase >= 1.0:
        phase -= 1.0
print([round(x, 4) for x in out])
```

```text
[0.0, 0.0576, 0.1149, 0.1719, 0.2284, 0.284]
```

This **phase accumulator** is the core of many digital oscillators. It has three advantages over recomputing phase from a growing sample counter.

**1. Frequency changes preserve phase.** Recomputing phase from total elapsed time with a new frequency can make the phase jump. Switch from 440 Hz to 450 Hz at 0.525 s:

```python
import math
fs = 48_000
t = 25_200 / fs      # 0.525 s
# Reusing absolute time changes the phase.
before = math.sin(2*math.pi*440*t)
after  = math.sin(2*math.pi*450*t)
print(f"{before:.3f} -> {after:.3f}")
```

```text
0.000 -> 1.000
```

At the switch time, the two formulas give values of 0 and full scale. Switching directly between them can introduce an abrupt waveform jump and an audible click; the exact adjacent samples and audibility depend on the switch and playback conditions. With an accumulator, you just change `inc` and the phase carries on from where it was. Vibrato, pitch bends and glides can use this. An abrupt increment change can still make a transient by changing the waveform’s slope; ramping the increment makes the transition gentler.

**2. Precision stays bounded.** The phase is always between 0 and 1, so its spacing stays bounded instead of getting coarser with elapsed time. Rounding of the increment and additions can still introduce a small frequency error. A sample counter n only grows. A 32-bit float (common on embedded chips) represents integers exactly only up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216. At 48 kHz that's about 349.5 seconds, under six minutes. At that boundary, adding one to a float32 counter can leave it unchanged. An oscillator relying on that counter can stall; other ever-growing time calculations can also lose phase accuracy.

**3. It's cheap.** One add and a compare per sample, then a waveform lookup. The waveform part can be `sin`, a table, or simple arithmetic for a sawtooth (the phase itself, rescaled, *is* a naive saw).

> [!warning] Keep the state between blocks
> Audio is processed in blocks (say 48 samples at a time). The phase must persist from one block to the next. Resetting it to zero each block repeats the same 48-sample segment. At 48 kHz, that repeated segment has a 1 kHz repetition rate, with spectral components on a 1 kHz grid, rather than the intended 440 Hz sine. Boundaries can jump and the result can buzz or click; the exact spectrum and audibility depend on the waveform, reset timing and playback conditions.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A clock hand changing speed
> A clock hand can speed up without jumping to a new position. It continues from wherever it has reached.
>
> **How it maps:** The hand’s position is oscillator phase; its speed is frequency. Changing the phase increment changes future progress while keeping the current phase.
>
> **Where it stops:** An oscillator’s phase wraps every cycle, and digital updates introduce rounding. A continuous phase also does not guarantee a perfectly smooth slope when its speed changes abruptly.

## Why absolute-time glides go wrong

Frequency is the rate at which phase advances. If you multiply a changing frequency by all the elapsed time, earlier cycles are effectively recalculated at the new frequency. This is the practical failure during a glide: The oscillator can run much faster than the setting suggests, and the error depends on when the glide begins. Frequencies pushed beyond Nyquist also alias in sampled playback. Accumulating only the new phase step avoids this recalculation of the past.

An accumulator adds each sample’s current increment to the phase already earned. It therefore follows the requested frequency sample by sample, subject to ordinary rounding error.

## Pitfalls

- **Ignoring wrap.** Without the wrap, a float phase eventually loses precision like the counter does.

## Key takeaways

- Keep phase as oscillator state and add the current increment for every sample.
- Changing the increment preserves phase; recomputing from absolute time can cause jumps.
- Wrap phase to keep numerical spacing bounded, and retain it between audio blocks. Rounding error still remains.

## Further reading

- [Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html)
- [Numerically controlled oscillator (phase accumulator) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerically_controlled_oscillator)
- [Changing frequency requires accumulated phase — CMU Introduction to Computer Music](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~music/icm-online/readings/fm-synthesis/index.html)

questions.prompt: An oscillator resets phase at the start of every audio block instead of preserving it. Why can the result buzz or click?

options.text: The requested note is always preserved exactly
options.explanation: Restarting phase replaces continuous oscillator progress with repeated truncated segments.

options.text: A block cannot contain fractional cycles
options.explanation: Fractional cycles across blocks are normal when phase state is retained.

options.text: The sample rate automatically rises at each reset
options.explanation: Resetting oscillator state does not change the hardware clock.

options.text: The same truncated segment repeats, often with a jump at block boundaries
options.explanation: Correct. The block repetition can impose its own spectrum instead of the intended continuous tone.

questions.workedExample: A block boundary is a processing boundary, rather than a musical restart. Resetting phase repeats the same fragment and may join incompatible values. Store phase with the oscillator so the next block continues where the previous one ended.

questions.prompt: An oscillator uses an ever-growing float32 sample counter and starts losing precision after running for a while. Which change addresses that cause?

options.text: Increase the counter’s value faster
options.explanation: Larger values have coarser float spacing, making the problem worse.

options.text: Keep a wrapped phase accumulator and update it each sample
options.explanation: Correct. Wrapping bounds the magnitude instead of allowing precision to worsen with elapsed time.

options.text: Reset phase at every block
options.explanation: That creates repeated waveform fragments and possible boundary clicks.

options.text: Assume the float’s large range guarantees unit steps forever
options.explanation: Range and precision differ: large representable values can have gaps wider than one.

questions.workedExample: Float32 can represent very large values without representing every neighbouring integer. As the counter grows, its spacing grows. Keeping phase bounded avoids that growing-magnitude problem, although increment and addition rounding still remain.

questions.prompt: An oscillator is playing 440 Hz and must change to 880 Hz partway through a note. Which methods avoid a sudden jump in the *output value* (a click)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the phase accumulator and set the increment to the 880 Hz value at once
options.explanation: Correct for the output-value discontinuity asked about: phase is retained. The abrupt change in slope can still create a transient; smoothing pitch makes the transition gentler.

options.text: Keep the phase accumulator and ramp the increment from the 440 Hz value to the 880 Hz value over 50 ms
options.explanation: Correct. This is a glide (portamento). The phase stays continuous throughout.

options.text: From the change onwards, compute `sin(2π·880·t)` using the absolute time t
options.explanation: Wrong: a 880 Hz sine and a 440 Hz sine both computed from absolute time are at unrelated phases at the moment of the switch, so the output generally jumps.

options.text: Reset the phase to 0 and start the 880 Hz cycle from there
options.explanation: Wrong: the output jumps from wherever the 440 Hz wave was to the sine of zero, which is 0. Unless the old wave happened to be at a zero crossing, that's a step.

questions.workedExample: An accumulator retains the current cycle position when the pitch changes. Changing its increment therefore preserves waveform value at the switch; ramping it also smooths the slope change. Recomputing from absolute time or resetting phase generally selects a different position and creates a step. Specially timed switches can coincide by chance, so neither method guarantees a step at every possible instant.

questions.prompt: A developer makes a glide by multiplying the current frequency by the total elapsed time to obtain phase. The glide sounds wrong, especially when triggered later in a recording. Why?

options.text: The frequency setting alone always gives the correct instantaneous frequency
options.explanation: Phase progress must accumulate the changing frequency; the setting times total time does not do that.

options.text: The target frequency is used before the glide begins
options.explanation: The issue is how phase is computed, even if the setting follows the intended glide.

options.text: Glides require a larger bit depth rather than phase state
options.explanation: Sample precision cannot repair the phase calculation.

options.text: Changing the current frequency also recalculates phase for all the past time
options.explanation: Correct. Accumulate each current phase increment instead, so only new progress uses the new frequency.

questions.workedExample: Frequency describes how fast phase should advance now. Multiplying a new frequency by total elapsed time changes the phase attributed to the whole history. This can produce excessive instantaneous frequency, which may then alias. Add each sample’s current increment to retained phase instead.

lessons.title: Pitch ratios and equal temperament
lessons.summary: Use doublings and logarithms to explain octaves and equal-tempered semitones.
lessons.body:
A synth receives "play note 60" and has to turn it into a phase increment. Between those two is a formula you'll write in your first afternoon and use for the rest of the project. Understanding it properly also explains why pitch bends, detune and vibrato are specified in semitones and cents, not hertz.

## Pitch is a ratio, not a difference

**Frequency** is physical: cycles per second. **Pitch** is perceptual: how high or low a note sounds. For a steady periodic tone, the pitch we hear closely tracks the **fundamental frequency** (the rate at which the whole waveform repeats).

The crucial fact is that our ears judge pitch by **ratios**. Going from 110 Hz to 220 Hz sounds like the same step as going from 440 Hz to 880 Hz, even though the first is a 110 Hz difference and the second is 440 Hz. Both are a doubling, and a doubling of frequency is an **octave**.

```text
A1    A2    A3    A4    A5
55 -> 110 -> 220 -> 440 -> 880 Hz
  x2    x2    x2    x2
```

So pitch is **logarithmic** in frequency: equal steps in pitch are equal *multiplications* of frequency. This is the basis of musical pitch arithmetic.

## Exponentials and logarithms, briefly

An exponential turns a pitch offset into a frequency ratio. One octave means doubling; two octaves means doubling twice. Fractional octaves fill the spaces between those steps. A base-2 logarithm works backwards: it counts how many doublings a positive frequency ratio represents.

Adding pitch offsets combines their ratios by multiplication. Up an octave and then up another octave doubles twice, regardless of the starting note. You do not need to memorise a logarithm identity to use this idea.

The practical rule follows: **do pitch arithmetic in note space, then convert to hertz once at the end.** In note space, transposing, bending and modulating are simple additions. In hertz they're multiplications, and mixing the two up is a classic bug.

## Semitones and equal temperament

Western chromatic music commonly divides the octave into 12 **semitones**. In **twelve-tone equal temperament** (12-TET), every semitone has the same frequency ratio. Twelve of them must make an octave (×2), so each one is the number that gives 2 when 12 copies of it are multiplied together.

Each semitone up multiplies frequency by about 1.0595; twelve such steps exactly double it.

For example, the note one semitone above A4 (440 Hz) is A♯4, at about 466.16 Hz.

Equal temperament gives every key the same interval pattern. That flexibility means most intervals differ slightly from pure whole-number ratios. Simple whole-number ratios such as 3:2 (the pure ratio of a perfect fifth) don't land exactly on a 12-TET note:

| Interval | Just ratio | 12-TET ratio | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Octave | 2.000 | 2.000 | 0 cents |
| Fifth | 1.500 | 1.4983 | 12-TET 1.96 cents flat |
| Major third | 1.250 | 1.2599 | 12-TET 13.69 cents sharp |

The difference column uses **cents**: hundredths of a semitone, explored in the tuning unit. 12-TET is a common default tuning; alternative tunings are a later feature.

## Pitfalls

- **Adding hertz for musical intervals.** "Up a fifth" is ×1.4983, not +220 Hz.

## Key takeaways

- An octave doubles frequency; musical intervals use ratios rather than fixed hertz differences.
- Exponentials turn octave offsets into ratios, and base-2 logarithms count doublings.
- In 12-TET, twelve identical semitone ratios multiply to two. Just intervals differ slightly.

## Further reading

- [Equal temperament — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_temperament)
- [Cent (music) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_(music))
- [Notes, MIDI numbers and frequencies — UNSW](https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/notes.html)

lessons.title: Convert MIDI notes to frequency
lessons.summary: Turn note numbers into hertz, invert the conversion and avoid integer-division and octave-label bugs.
lessons.body:
## MIDI note numbers

MIDI identifies notes with a number from **0 to 127**. Note **60 is middle C**, and **69 is the A above it**, which is tuned to **440 Hz** by convention. Each step of 1 is one semitone. Your synth needs to turn a note number into a frequency, and the usual equal-tempered conversion follows those ratios:

```formula reference
f = 440 × 2^((n − 69) / 12)
where
f: the frequency to play, in hertz (Hz)
n: the MIDI note number, 0 to 127 (or a fractional value once bends and detune are added); here 60, middle C
440: the reference frequency of note 69 (A4), in hertz
69: the note number of A4, the reference note
12: semitones per octave
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: With equal-tempered tuning and A4 at 440 hertz, count semitones from note 69, turn them into octave steps, then apply that frequency ratio to 440 hertz.
```

Going the other way, a tuner or a pitch detector turns a frequency back into a (usually fractional) note number:

```formula reference
n = 69 + 12 log_2(f / 440)
where
n: the note number, fractional in general; the nearest whole number is the nearest note
f: the measured frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 880 Hz
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which counts doublings
440: the reference frequency of A4, in hertz
69: the note number of A4
12: semitones per octave
In words: To estimate a note number, count octave ratios from the reference A, turn those into semitones and add them to note 69. The nearest whole number is the nearest equal-tempered note.
```

Both conversions assume 12-TET with A4 at 440 Hz. Changing the reference pitch changes the frequency scale; a different tuning system may require a different mapping altogether.

```python
def midi_to_hz(n, a4=440.0):
    # Semitone offset becomes a ratio.
    return a4 * 2 ** ((n - 69) / 12)

for n in (0, 21, 57, 60, 69, 81, 108, 127):
    print(f"{n:>3} {midi_to_hz(n):9.2f} Hz")
```

```text
  0      8.18 Hz
 21     27.50 Hz
 57    220.00 Hz
 60    261.63 Hz
 69    440.00 Hz
 81    880.00 Hz
108   4186.01 Hz
127  12543.85 Hz
```

Notes 21 to 108 are the 88 keys of a piano (A0 to C8). Note 0, at about 8.2 Hz, is below hearing; you'd hear it only through its harmonics.

> [!warning] Octave labels vary, numbers don't
> In scientific pitch notation middle C is **C4**, so note 60 = C4 and 69 = A4. Some software and instruments label note 60 as C3 instead: Ableton Live’s manual gives its full MIDI range as C−2 to G8, which places note 60 at C3. The number on the wire is always 60, so think in note numbers and check how each piece of gear displays them.

Keep the 440 as a parameter (`a4` above). A "master tune" control is just a different reference.

## Pitfalls

- **Integer division.** In C-family languages, `(n − 69) / 12` with integers truncates to whole octaves. Use floating point.
- **Assuming octave labels.** Use note numbers between systems.

## Key takeaways

- The conventional 12-TET reference is note 69 at 440 Hz, with one semitone per note-number step.
- Use floating-point division in the exponent and keep the reference pitch configurable.
- Note 60 is middle C; displayed octave names vary between products.

## Further reading

- [MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_tuning_standard)
- [MIDI 1.0 core specifications — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-core-specifications)
- [Piano key frequencies — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_key_frequencies)
- [Sampler key range — Ableton Live 12 manual](https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-instrument-reference/)
- [Tuning reference and note mapping — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/microtuning-and-alternative-intonation-systems)
- [Notes, MIDI numbers and frequencies — UNSW](https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/notes.html)

questions.prompt:
A developer writes the MIDI-to-frequency formula in a language where `/` between two integers truncates towards zero, with `n` an integer:

```c

```

What does note 60 come out as?

options.explanation: That's the correct value, but it needs a fractional exponent (−0.75). Integer division throws the fraction away.

options.explanation: That would need the exponent to round down to −1 (floor division). Truncation *towards zero* gives 0.

options.text: An error: you can't raise 2 to a negative power
options.explanation: 2 to a negative power is fine (2⁻¹ = 0.5). The bug is silent, which is what makes it dangerous.

options.explanation: Correct. (60 − 69)/12 = −9/12 truncates to 0, and 440 × 2⁰ = 440. Every note from 58 to 80 plays A4, and the others snap to whole octaves of A.

questions.workedExample:

2. −9 / 12 as integers, truncated towards zero → 0 (the exact value is −0.75).
3. 2⁰ = 1, so the frequency is 440 × 1 = **440 Hz**.

Notes 58–80 all give an exponent of 0, notes 81–92 give 1 (880 Hz), and so on. Fix it by making the division floating point (12.0). Python's `/` always returns a float, which is why the lesson's Python works; Python's `//` would floor to −1 and give 220 Hz.

lessons.title: Cents, tuning errors and beats
lessons.summary: Express tuning errors in cents and predict the beat rate of two close tones.
lessons.body:
## Cents

A **cent** is 1/100 of a 12-TET semitone, so there are 1200 cents per octave. To measure how far apart two frequencies are in pitch, count the octaves between them and multiply by 1200:

```formula reference
c = 1200 log_2(f_2 / f_1)
where
c: the interval from f_1 up to f_2, in cents (negative if f_2 is lower)
f_1: the reference frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 440 Hz
f_2: the other frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 445 Hz
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which counts octaves in a frequency ratio
cents: hundredths of a semitone; 1200 make an octave
In words: compare the frequency ratio to count pitch distance in cents. A higher second frequency gives a positive interval; a lower one gives a negative interval.
```

To apply a cents detune, multiply by the ratio for that interval. The reference conversion is:

```formula reference
f_2 = f_1 × 2^(c / 1200)
where
f_2: the shifted frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_1: the starting frequency, in hertz (Hz)
c: the shift in cents (positive is sharp, negative is flat)
In words: A fixed cents offset multiplies every starting frequency by the same ratio: positive cents sharpen it and negative cents flatten it.
```

How small is a cent? It is often smaller than a pitch change a listener can reliably distinguish between separate tones. The just-noticeable difference depends on frequency, duration, level, timbre, training and the listener. Research finds substantial variation with test conditions, so use measured results for the particular listening task. Two tones played together are another matter: even a cent or two of mistuning can be heard as slow beating.

Cents are the natural unit for **detune**. Here's a function that finds the nearest note and how far off it is:

```python
import math

NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F",
         "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]

def hz_to_note(f, a4=440.0):
    # Keep the fractional note for detune.
    m = 69 + 12 * math.log2(f / a4)
    n = round(m)
    # Report error from the nearest note.
    cents = 100 * (m - n)
    name = NAMES[n % 12] + str(n // 12 - 1)
    return n, name, cents

for f in (261.63, 450.0, 430.0, 100.0):
    n, name, c = hz_to_note(f)
    tag = f"{c:+.1f}c"
    print(f"{f:.2f} ->", n, name, tag)
```

```text
261.63 -> 60 C4 +0.0c
450.00 -> 69 A4 +38.9c
430.00 -> 69 A4 -39.8c
100.00 -> 43 G2 +35.0c
```

The `n // 12 − 1` gives the octave number in scientific pitch notation, because note 0 is C−1.

## Detuning and beats

Play two oscillators at nearly the same frequency and you hear the level wobble. That's **beating**: the two sines drift in and out of phase, reinforcing then cancelling. The wobble happens once for every cycle one oscillator gains on the other, so its rate is the difference in frequency. For example, detuning one 440 Hz oscillator by +10 cents produces about 442.55 Hz. The pair beats about 2.55 times per second.

The frequency difference describes the interference envelope. A difference of a few hertz sounds like a slow level wobble. As the difference grows into tens of hertz, listeners may hear rapid beats, roughness or two distinct tones rather than a countable wobble. The perceptual boundaries depend on the tones and listener.

Because the detune is in cents, the *beat rate* grows with pitch: the same 10 cents at 880 Hz beats at about 5.1 Hz. This is why a fixed-cents detune sounds "wider" in the high register, and some synths offer a fixed-Hz detune as an alternative.

## Key takeaways

- A semitone contains 100 cents, and an octave contains 1200.
- Use a logarithm to measure an interval and an exponential to apply detune.
- Two close tones beat at their frequency difference; fixed-cents detune beats faster on higher notes.

## Further reading

- [Cent (music) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_(music))
- [Pitch discrimination and harmonicity — Micheyl, Ryan & Oxenham](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356318/)
- [Beats and their perception — UNSW Physclips](https://www.animations.physics.unsw.edu.au/jw/beats.htm)
- [Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(acoustics))

lessons.title: Vibrato and pitch-space arithmetic
lessons.summary: Compare fixed-hertz and fixed-cents vibrato and combine bend, detune and modulation before conversion.
lessons.body:
## Linear vs exponential modulation

Suppose an LFO adds vibrato. Two ways to do it:

1. **Linear (in Hz):** add a fixed number of hertz.
2. **Exponential (in pitch):** multiply by a fixed ratio, set in cents.

```formula reference
f_lin = f_0 + D × L
f_exp = f_0 × 2^(d × L / 1200)
where
f_lin: the frequency with linear (hertz) vibrato, in hertz (Hz)
f_exp: the frequency with exponential (pitch) vibrato, in hertz (Hz)
f_0: the note's unmodulated frequency, in hertz (Hz)
L: the LFO's current output, swinging between −1 and +1
D: the linear vibrato depth, in hertz (Hz); for example 10 Hz
d: the exponential vibrato depth, in cents; for example 39 cents
In words: linear vibrato swings the frequency by the same number of hertz on every note; exponential vibrato swings it by the same musical interval on every note.
```

A fixed 10 Hz swing is a much larger fraction of a 110 Hz bass note than of a 440 Hz note. Its musical interval is therefore wider in the bass. Specifying a fixed cents depth instead gives the same pitch interval in each register.

Option 2 is what players expect for vibrato and pitch bend. MIDI pitch bend, for example, is normally interpreted as a number of semitones (the bend range), added in note space.

Analogue synths face the same problem in hardware. The common **1 volt per octave** standard, used by Moog instruments, makes control voltage linear in pitch: each extra volt doubles the oscillator frequency, using an exponential converter inside the oscillator.

For example, two extra volts request two octaves: a 110 Hz oscillator would ideally become 440 Hz. A semitone needs one twelfth of a volt. Real oscillators follow this law only over a limited range, which is why analogue synths need calibrating.

## Pitfalls

- **Converting too early.** Keep pitch as a float note number (including bend, detune and modulation in semitones), then convert to hertz, then to a phase increment.

## Key takeaways

- Fixed-hertz modulation changes its musical depth across the keyboard.
- Fixed-cents modulation applies the same interval on every note.
- Add bend, detune and modulation in note space, then convert to frequency and phase increment.

## Further reading

- [MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_tuning_standard)
- [CV/gate — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CV/gate)

lessons.title: Harmonics, timbre and missing fundamentals
lessons.summary: Separate pitch from harmonic content and explain beating between equal-tempered notes and harmonics.
lessons.body:
## Pitch vs timbre

Play a sine and a sawtooth at 220 Hz. They have the **same pitch** but sound completely different. The difference is **timbre**, often loosely called "tone colour".

A sawtooth at 220 Hz contains sine components at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on: the **harmonic series**, every whole-number multiple of the fundamental. In an ideal sawtooth their amplitudes fall off steadily.

The second harmonic is twice the fundamental frequency, the third is three times it, and so on. In an ideal sawtooth, the second has half the fundamental’s amplitude and the third one third. Higher harmonics grow weaker but enrich the waveform’s shape.

A sine has only the 220 Hz component. Because all the extra components are exact multiples, the waveform still repeats 220 times per second, and the ear still hears 220 Hz.

The harmonic series is also where just ratios come from: harmonics 2, 3, 4, 5 give an octave, a fifth above that, another octave, and a major third. The 5th harmonic of 110 Hz is 550 Hz, about 14 cents below the 12-TET C♯5 (554.37 Hz).

Timbre also depends on how the sound changes over time: the attack, how harmonics fade, noise. Subtractive synthesis works by starting with a harmonically rich wave and filtering harmonics away, changing timbre while leaving pitch alone. That's the next module.

> [!note] The missing fundamental
> Pitch perception isn't just "find the lowest component". If you remove the 220 Hz component from a sawtooth and keep 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on, most listeners still hear a pitch of 220 Hz, because the harmonics are spaced 220 Hz apart. This is why small speakers can suggest bass notes they can't reproduce.

## Key takeaways

- A periodic waveform’s harmonics lie at whole-number multiples of its fundamental.
- Harmonic amplitudes and changes over time shape timbre.
- Listeners can hear a missing fundamental from the spacing of the remaining harmonics.

## Further reading

- [Equal temperament — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_temperament)
- [Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(acoustics))
- [Timbre — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre)

options.explanation: Beating is heard between components that are *close* in frequency. 110 Hz and 554 Hz are over two octaves apart; their difference is not heard as a wobble.

options.explanation: Mixing adds samples and creates no new spectral frequencies by itself. Existing close components can still interfere and beat; that is the wobble here.

options.explanation: Pitch isn't an average of components. Perception follows the common period of the waveform.

lessons.title: Sample timing, block deadlines and memory
lessons.summary: Interpret sample instants and budget processing time, buffer memory and audio data rate.
lessons.body:
A digital synth handles a timed stream of numbers, and a converter turns it into an analogue voltage. This lesson is about what those numbers are, how precise they need to be, and what goes wrong at the edges.

Two separate settings decide the quality of a digital signal. **Sample rate** sets how *often* you measure. **Bit depth** sets how *finely* each measurement is recorded. Neither of them is the playback volume, which is decided by the numbers' size relative to full scale and by whatever amplifier follows the converter.

## Discrete-time signals

**Sampling a signal** means measuring a continuous signal at evenly spaced instants. The spacing between instants is the sample period, so each sample index identifies one measurement time.

At 48 kHz, sample instants are about 20.8 microseconds apart. Sample indices count these instants from zero; dividing the index by the rate gives its time in seconds.

Picture each sample as a lollipop: a value at an instant, with nothing defined in between.

```diagram
  |   o
  |   |  o
  | o |  |
  | | |  |     time ->
--+-+-+--+--+--+--
  |          |  |
  |          |  o
  |          o
```

A sample is a value at an instant, rather than a little rectangle of constant value. Ideal band-limited reconstruction determines the smooth signal from those samples; real DACs approximate this using their reconstruction filters.

Common sample rates:

| Rate | Typical use |
|---|---|
| 44.1 kHz | CD audio |
| 48 kHz | Video, most pro audio and audio hardware |
| 96 kHz | High-resolution recording; some synth internals |

The sample rate fixes the **highest frequency** you can represent: half the sample rate, as the Nyquist-limit unit explains. At 48 kHz the ideal reconstruction band lies strictly below 24 kHz, above the roughly 20 kHz limit of hearing. Higher rates mostly buy room for processing that creates high frequencies (distortion, sharp waveforms), not extra audible treble.

It also sets your **time budget**. Synths process audio in blocks (a fixed number of samples handled in one go), and the hardware plays a block in a fixed time:

```formula reference
t_b = N_b / fs
where
t_b: the duration of one block, in seconds (s)
N_b: the block size, in samples; here 48
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a block lasts its number of samples divided by the sample rate, so 48 samples at 48 kHz is 1 ms.
```

All the work for a block must finish in less time than that, every time. If it doesn't, the hardware runs out of samples and you hear a click or dropout.

## How much data is that?

The numbers add up quickly, which matters on a microcontroller:

```formula reference
M = fs × t × B × C
R = fs × b × C
where
M: the memory needed, in bytes
R: the data rate, in bits per second (bit/s)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
t: the length of audio, in seconds; here 1
B: bytes per sample; 4 for float32
b: bits per sample; here 24
C: the number of channels; 1 for mono, 2 for stereo
bytes: units of 8 bits
bit/s: bits per second
In words: Buffer memory grows with sample rate, duration, bytes per sample and channels. Unpacked audio data rate grows with sample rate, bits per sample and channels.
```

- One second of mono float32 at 48 kHz is 192,000 bytes, about 192 kB (kilobytes).
- Stereo 24-bit audio data at 48 kHz is 2.304 Mbit/s (megabits per second). On an I²S bus, 24-bit samples often travel in 32-bit slots, giving a 3.072 MHz bit clock for two such slots per sample frame. Check the actual interface configuration.

A delay effect with a two-second buffer needs 384,000 bytes (384 kB) per channel in float32. Check this against your board's RAM before designing features.

## Pitfalls

- **Confusing the three settings.** Sample rate (how often), bit depth (how finely), level (how big relative to full scale). Turning a synth down in software doesn't change its bit depth, but very quiet *integer* signals do use fewer effective bits.

## Key takeaways

- Sample rate determines the spacing of sample instants and the duration of each processing block.
- Finish each block before the hardware consumes it or audio can drop out.
- Buffer memory scales with duration, sample rate, bytes per sample and channel count.

## Further reading

- [Sampling (signal processing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(signal_processing))

lessons.title: Integer levels and rounding error
lessons.summary: Explain how bit depth changes level spacing and distinguish rounding error from clipping.
lessons.body:
## Bit depth and quantisation

Each sample must be stored with finite precision. Every extra bit doubles the number of patterns available to represent a sample.

For example, 16 bits provide 65,536 distinct levels. A signed sample uses some codes for negative values, one for zero and the rest for positive values; it does not lose half its precision by being signed.

| Bits | Levels | Integer range |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 256 | −128 to 127 |
| 16 | 65,536 | −32,768 to 32,767 |
| 24 | 16,777,216 | −8,388,608 to 8,388,607 |

Rounding the true value to the nearest level is **quantisation**. The levels are evenly spaced, so the step size is the width of the range divided by the number of levels, and rounding to the nearest level is wrong by at most half a step either way:

```formula reference
Δ = 2 / 2^N
e_max = Δ / 2
where
Δ: delta, the quantisation step size: the gap between neighbouring levels, in full-scale units
2: the width of the range from −1 to +1 (full scale)
N: the bit depth, in bits; here 16
e_max: the largest possible rounding error when rounding to the nearest level
In words: For signed samples scaled around minus one to plus one, each extra bit halves the gap between levels. Nearest rounding stays within half a gap when the signal does not overload.
```

This assumes the signal stays inside full scale; a value beyond the top or bottom level is clipped, and its error can be much larger.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Rounding a length to ruler marks
> A ruler with finer marks lets you report a length more closely. Rounding to the nearest mark moves the report by no more than half the gap between marks.
>
> **How it maps:** Ruler marks are integer sample levels; adding a bit makes the marks twice as dense across the same full-scale range. Nearest rounding chooses the closest available level.
>
> **Where it stops:** An audio sample can be negative, and its signed endpoints are asymmetric. Values beyond the available range overload rather than simply rounding to a nearby internal mark.

## Pitfalls

- **Truncating instead of rounding.** Truncation toward zero gives sign-dependent error approaching a full step; it need not add DC to a symmetric signal. Rounding downward instead has a negative bias, averaging about half a step under the uniform-error model. Nearest rounding limits error to half a step away from overload.

## Key takeaways

- Each extra bit doubles the number of distinct integer sample values.
- Nearest rounding stays within half a step away from overload.
- Signed integer endpoints are asymmetric; overload and truncation require separate care.

## Further reading

- [Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(signal_processing))
- [Audio bit depth — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_bit_depth)
- [Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-001.pdf)

0.3 × 4 = 1.2 rounds to 1, not 2, so the result is 0.25.

lessons.title: Predict and measure quantisation noise
lessons.summary: Use the six-decibel-per-bit rule and recognise when coarse quantisation violates its assumptions.
lessons.body:
## Quantisation noise and the six-decibel rule

For a busy signal much larger than one step, the error behaves like a small random noise added to the signal: **quantisation noise**. How far that noise sits below the signal is the **SQNR**, the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio, measured in decibels (dB, a logarithmic scale for ratios explained in the decibel-gain unit). The standard result, for a full-scale sine wave, is:

```formula reference
SQNR ≈ 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB
where
SQNR: signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio: the RMS (average) level of a full-scale sine compared with the RMS level of the rounding noise, in decibels
N: the bit depth, in bits; here 16
dB: decibels; every 6 dB is roughly a factor of 2 in amplitude
≈: approximately equal to (the formula is an approximation, and the result is rounded)
In words: each bit adds about 6 dB of distance between a full-scale sine and the quantisation noise, plus a constant 1.76 dB, so 16 bits give about 98 dB.
```

**Each extra bit adds about 6 dB**, because it halves the step size and halving an amplitude is −6.02 dB. 16 bits gives about 98 dB; 24 bits about 146 dB.

The six-decibel rule assumes a sine that nearly fills full scale without overloading and rounding error that is approximately uniform and unrelated to the signal. A quieter signal sits closer to the same quantisation floor. Coarse periodic signals can instead produce correlated distortion. The Analog Devices tutorial derives the result in detail.

You can check this in a few lines:

```python
import numpy as np

fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(fs)                 # 1 second
x = 0.999 * np.sin(2*np.pi*997*n/fs)

def quantise(x, bits):
    scale = 2 ** (bits - 1)  # 16 -> 32768
    # Round to the nearest integer level.
    q = np.round(x * scale)
    # Saturate at the signed endpoints.
    q = np.clip(q, -scale, scale - 1)
    return q / scale

for bits in (4, 8, 12, 16):
    # Compare quantised samples to input.
    err = quantise(x, bits) - x
    snr = 10*np.log10(np.mean(x**2)
                      / np.mean(err**2))
    pred = 6.02*bits + 1.76
    print(f"{bits:>2} bits: {snr:5.1f} dB"
          f" (formula {pred:5.1f})")
```

```text
 4 bits:  23.3 dB (formula  25.8)
 8 bits:  49.3 dB (formula  49.9)
12 bits:  74.0 dB (formula  74.0)
16 bits:  98.1 dB (formula  98.1)
```

At 12 and 16 bits the formula agrees closely. At 4 bits this example also **overloads the positive endpoint**: its largest code is 7/8, below the sine's 0.999 peak. That clipping contributes substantial error. In addition, the uniform, signal-independent error model is only an approximation; low-resolution periodic quantisation can produce distortion rather than a gentle hiss.

> [!note] Why 997 Hz?
> Test tones are often slightly "odd" frequencies like 997 Hz rather than 1000 Hz. With 1000 Hz at 48 kHz, each cycle is exactly 48 samples, so the same few quantisation errors repeat every cycle and pile up at harmonic frequencies. A tone without that short repeating sample pattern can distribute quantisation error more broadly; the relation between test frequency and sample rate matters, rather than whether a number is odd.

## Key takeaways

- The uniform-error model predicts about 6.02 dB per bit plus 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine.
- Lower signal level reduces SQNR even when the file’s bit depth stays fixed.
- Coarse quantisation and endpoint overload can produce distortion and disagree with the noise model.

## Further reading

- [Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(signal_processing))
- [Audio bit depth — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_bit_depth)
- [Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-001.pdf)

lessons.title: Dither and converter noise floors
lessons.summary: Explain why reducing bit depth needs dither and why a converter’s word length exceeds its effective resolution.
lessons.body:
## Dither and real converter noise

The same problem returns for **very quiet signals**, even at 16 bits. A sine whose amplitude is under half a step rounds to zero every time and vanishes completely. A fade-out turns gritty in its last few bits.

**Dither** addresses this by adding a tiny amount of random noise *before* quantising. Common triangular (TPDF) dither spans two quantisation steps peak-to-peak. With suitable dither and no overload, the output error’s mean and noise power no longer vary with the signal: you trade extra hiss for removal of systematic quantisation distortion, and quiet details survive statistically inside the noise. This does not mean every property of the total error is independent of the signal. Dither matters whenever you **reduce** bit depth, such as when exporting 16-bit files. Inside a 32-bit float synth it's rarely needed.

### Real converters

A "24-bit" converter outputs 24-bit words, but its analogue noise floor is far above the theoretical 146 dB. Examples from TI’s datasheets are 99 dB typical for the PCM1808 ADC and 112 dB typical for the PCM5102A DAC. These are A-weighted figures under the stated test conditions. The higher-performance PCM1792A specifies 127 dB with a 2 V RMS stereo test output and 132 dB in its mono test configuration. These are different configurations, not a guaranteed range for any board. Board circuitry and power supplies affect the result, so check the datasheet and measure. 24 bits gives a comfortable margin so that converter noise, not quantisation, sets the floor.

A noise-only estimate of effective resolution can be obtained by rearranging the full-scale-sine SQNR rule from the preceding unit. Formal ENOB measurements normally use SINAD, which includes distortion as well as noise; substituting an A-weighted dynamic-range figure gives only an estimate.

## Key takeaways

- Dither adds noise before quantisation to decorrelate error from quiet signals.
- Use dither when reducing bit depth; continuous float processing usually does not need it.
- A 24-bit converter’s analogue noise floor is higher than ideal 24-bit quantisation noise. Check and measure the hardware.

## Further reading

- [Dither — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dither)
- [Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-001.pdf)
- [PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/pcm5102a.pdf)
- [PCM1808 ADC datasheet — Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/pcm1808.pdf)
- [PCM1792A DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/pcm1792a.pdf)
- [SINAD, SNR and ENOB — Analog Devices MT-003](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-003.pdf)

lessons.title: Float headroom and integer conversion
lessons.summary: Keep internal float headroom and convert safely at fixed-format boundaries.
lessons.body:
## The −1..1 convention and floating point

Inside most audio software, samples are **floating-point numbers where ±1.0 means full scale**. The converter's maximum output corresponds to 1.0. This convention lets the same code work whatever bit depth the hardware uses.

Why floats internally?

- **Headroom.** A float can hold 3.7 or −12.0 without trouble. Mixing several voices can exceed 1.0 mid-chain and be scaled down later without clipping; normal floating-point rounding still applies. Integers would overflow or clip.
- **Resolution where it matters.** A 32-bit float has a 24-bit significand plus an exponent. Quiet signals in the normal range keep their relative precision, because the exponent scales with the value; subnormal values lose significant bits.
- **Simple maths.** Gain is a multiply; mixing is an add.

Integer and **fixed-point arithmetic** formats still matter at the edges: WAV files, converter interfaces, and microcontrollers without a floating-point unit. The conversion at the boundary is where bugs live:

```python
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0.5, -0.25, 1.0, -1.0, 1.7])
r = np.clip(np.round(x * 32767),
            -32768, 32767)
# Cast only after rounding and clipping.
i16 = r.astype(np.int16)
print(i16)
# Decode using a different scale: a loss.
y = i16 / 32768
print(np.round(y, 5).tolist())
```

```text
[ 16384  -8192  32767 -32767  32767]
[0.5, -0.25, 0.99997, -0.99997, 0.99997]
```

Three things to notice:

1. **1.7 was clipped** to 32767. Over-range floats must be clipped at conversion, never cast directly. In C and C++, converting a float to an integer type that can't hold its value is undefined behaviour. In practice you may get a wrapped value or, on x86, the "integer indefinite" value −2,147,483,648: either way, a loud crack. NumPy is no safer: in testing, `np.array([1.7 * 32767]).astype(np.int16)` gave −9833, silently.
2. **Asymmetry.** Integers run from −32768 to +32767, so full scale isn't symmetric. Libraries choose 32767 or 32768 as the scale factor.
3. **Inconsistent scale factors.** Here the code multiplied by 32767 but divided by 32768, so a round trip shrinks the signal very slightly. Pick one convention and use it both ways.

## Pitfalls

- **Casting instead of clipping** at float-to-integer conversion.
- **Denormals.** Float values extremely close to zero (subnormals, or denormals) are much slower to process on some processors: some x86 instructions on some processors need a slow assist, costing tens or hundreds of cycles. The penalty depends on the processor, instruction and floating-point mode; benchmark the target rather than assuming a fixed cost. Decaying filters and reverbs can produce them. The usual fixes are to switch on the CPU's flush-to-zero (and denormals-are-zero) mode for the audio thread, as many audio frameworks do, or to add a tiny offset or noise so the values never get that small.

## Key takeaways

- With floats, ±1 is nominal full scale and intermediate results can exceed it.
- Clamp over-range values before integer conversion and use consistent scale factors.
- Float precision follows the signal’s scale, but subnormal values can have processor-specific performance costs.

## Further reading

- [Single-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-precision_floating-point_format)
- [Subnormal number — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subnormal_number)
- [Subnormal numbers — Intel documentation](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/fortran-compiler/developer-guide-reference/2024-2/subnormal-numbers.html)
- [Floating-to-integer conversion — C++ standard draft](https://eel.is/c++draft/conv.fpint)

lessons.title: The Nyquist limit and ambiguous samples
lessons.summary: Explain why sufficiently band-limited signals reconstruct exactly and why frequencies beyond Nyquist become ambiguous.
lessons.body:
Sampling has a hard limit. Above a certain frequency, a sampled signal stops meaning what you think it means: a 30 kHz tone and an 18 kHz tone can produce *exactly the same samples*. This is **digital aliasing**, usually just called aliasing, and it's the most important limitation in digital synthesis.

For a synth builder it's not an abstract worry. The classic analogue waveforms (sawtooth, square, pulse) have harmonics that go on for ever. Generate them naively in software and some of those harmonics fold back into the audible range as clangy, out-of-tune tones. This lesson explains why, and how to predict exactly where they'll land.

## The sampling theorem

The **Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem** says:

A strictly band-limited signal can be reconstructed ideally when the sample rate is more than twice its highest frequency. This requires all frequency content to remain below the boundary, including harmonics.

The practical boundary is half the sample rate, called the Nyquist frequency. At 48 kHz that boundary is 24 kHz; the signal’s content must stay strictly below it for unambiguous ideal reconstruction.

Some common rates and their boundaries:

| Sample rate | Nyquist frequency |
|---|---|
| 44.1 kHz | 22.05 kHz |
| 48 kHz | 24 kHz |
| 96 kHz | 48 kHz |

"Perfectly reconstructed" is a strong claim and it's true. Below Nyquist, samples aren't a rough approximation of the wave: they contain all its information. A 10 kHz sine at 48 kHz has only 4.8 samples per cycle and looks like a jagged mess on a plot, yet ideal reconstruction rebuilds a pure 10 kHz sine from those samples. Real DACs approximate the ideal with finite filters, finite precision and analogue noise.

The condition is strict: *below* half the sample rate, rather than at it. A sine exactly at the boundary gets sampled twice per cycle. Depending on its phase, the samples might be +1, −1, +1, −1 or 0, 0, 0, 0. They can't tell you the amplitude.

## What aliasing is

Take a sine at 30 kHz and sample it at 48 kHz. Its phase moves more than half a cycle per sample. Because whole turns leave no trace in the sine value, the samples can equally describe a lower-frequency sine moving in the opposite phase direction. At this rate, they match an inverted 18 kHz sine:

```python
import numpy as np
fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(8)
hi = np.sin(2*np.pi*30_000*n/fs)
lo = np.sin(2*np.pi*18_000*n/fs)
# True means equal samples after inversion.
print(np.allclose(hi, -lo))
```

```text
True
```

The 30 kHz samples equal the 18 kHz samples with the sign flipped (a phase inversion). Once sampled, nothing can tell them apart. A DAC reconstructing the baseband will output the 18 kHz component. The 30 kHz tone has taken on an **alias frequency**, or alias.

## Key takeaways

- The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate; the reconstruction condition is strictly below it.
- A band-limited wave’s samples retain its information even when a plot looks jagged.
- Above-Nyquist tones can produce the same samples as lower tones, so their original frequency is lost.

## Further reading

- [Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sampling_Theorem.html)
- [Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyquist%E2%80%93Shannon_sampling_theorem)
- [Aliasing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliasing)

lessons.title: Predict where aliases fold
lessons.summary: Wrap a component by the sample rate, reflect it below Nyquist and trace rising-frequency sweeps.
lessons.body:
## Following an alias frequency

Picture the frequency axis folded back and forth like a paper fan, with creases at every multiple of the Nyquist frequency (fs/2 in the drawing, where fs is the sample rate):

```diagram
 0      fs/2      fs      3fs/2
 |--------|--------|--------|
 0 ----> 24k
         24k <---- 48k
                  48k ----> 72k
```

Any frequency maps to the point directly below it on the first segment, from 0 up to the Nyquist frequency. As a procedure:

1. Divide the frequency by the sample rate and keep the remainder (this is "modulo"), giving a value from 0 up to the sample rate.
2. If the result is above the Nyquist frequency, subtract it from the sample rate.

This reference rule implements that procedure. It predicts the folded frequency; phase still affects the signed waveform and special fold-point samples.

```formula reference
r = f mod fs
f_a = min(r, fs − r)
where
f: the true frequency being sampled, in hertz (Hz); here 30 kHz
fs: the sample rate, in hertz (Hz); here 48 kHz
mod: "modulo": the remainder after removing as many whole multiples of fs as possible (50,000 mod 48,000 is 2,000)
r: the frequency after wrapping into the range 0 up to fs
min: the smaller of the two values
f_a: the alias, the frequency that actually appears after sampling, between 0 and fs/2, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: wrap the frequency into one sample-rate's width, then, if it lands in the top half, reflect it down off the Nyquist frequency. 30 kHz sampled at 48 kHz appears at 18 kHz.
```

The formula holds for any frequency, sine by sine. A complex sound is a sum of sines, so apply it to each component separately.

```python
def alias(f, fs):
    f = f % fs          # wrap into [0, fs)
    # Reflect the upper half below Nyquist.
    return fs - f if f > fs / 2 else f

fs = 48_000
for f in (1_000, 23_000, 30_000, 47_000,
          50_000, 97_000):
    a = alias(f, fs)
    print(f"{f:>6} Hz -> {a:>6} Hz")
```

```text
  1000 Hz ->   1000 Hz
 23000 Hz ->  23000 Hz
 30000 Hz ->  18000 Hz
 47000 Hz ->   1000 Hz
 50000 Hz ->   2000 Hz
 97000 Hz ->   1000 Hz
```

The examples show that a very high input can appear near the bottom of the audio band. Removing whole sample-rate multiples first handles frequencies beyond the first fold.

Notice the behaviour as an input sweeps upwards: the alias rises to 24 kHz, then **falls** to 0 at 48 kHz, then rises again. A rising pitch whose alias falls is the unmistakable sound of aliasing.

## Key takeaways

- Take the frequency’s remainder after division by the sample rate.
- Reflect remainders above half the sample rate back into the lower half.
- Compute complex sounds component by component; aliases reverse direction at fold points.

## Further reading

- [Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sampling_Theorem.html)
- [Aliasing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliasing)

lessons.title: Why naive sawtooths and squares alias
lessons.summary: Explain why waveform edges create aliases and why folded harmonics can fall below the note.
lessons.body:
## Why sharp waveforms alias

A sine has one frequency. A sawtooth has harmonics at every whole-number multiple of its frequency, and their amplitudes fall slowly.

A sawtooth’s second harmonic has half the fundamental’s amplitude, its third one third and so on. Even the twentieth is only about 26 dB below the fundamental, so very high harmonics cannot simply be assumed inaudible.

A square has only the odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …), whose amplitudes also fall as one over the harmonic number. That fall-off is slow, so a lot of energy sits in very high harmonics.

The cause is the waveform's **sharp edge**. A discontinuity (an instant jump) needs infinitely many harmonics to describe, and a waveform with a jump has harmonic amplitudes that halve per octave of harmonic number (about 6 dB). A triangle wave has corners but no jumps; its harmonic amplitudes fall fourfold per octave (about 12 dB), so it aliases far less.

A **naive sawtooth** is generated directly from the phase accumulator (the phase-accumulator unit) by rescaling the phase.

Rescaling the wrapped phase from zero-to-one into minus-one-to-plus-one creates a rising ramp. At each wrap it jumps straight from the top back to the bottom: that is the naive sawtooth’s sharp edge.

That jump makes it a sample of the ideal infinite-bandwidth sawtooth. Every harmonic above Nyquist folds back. Take a high note, 1760 Hz (A6), at 48 kHz:

- Harmonics up to the thirteenth (22,880 Hz) are below 24 kHz and fine.
- Harmonics 14 and up fold back; **many land away from multiples of 1760 Hz**. Some higher aliases can also coincide with genuine harmonic bins.

Which aliases land low, where they are most audible?

```python
import math

def alias(f, fs):
    f = f % fs
    # Reflect the upper half below Nyquist.
    return fs - f if f > fs / 2 else f

fs, f0 = 48_000, 1_760
for k in range(14, 31):
    a = alias(k * f0, fs)
    # Show low aliases likely to be audible.
    if a < 5_000:
        # Level of this source harmonic.
        db = 20 * math.log10(1 / k)
        print(f"harmonic {k}: {k*f0} Hz"
              f" -> {a} Hz ({db:.1f} dB)")
```

```text
harmonic 25: 44000 Hz -> 4000 Hz (-28.0 dB)
harmonic 26: 45760 Hz -> 2240 Hz (-28.3 dB)
harmonic 27: 47520 Hz -> 480 Hz (-28.6 dB)
harmonic 28: 49280 Hz -> 1280 Hz (-28.9 dB)
harmonic 29: 51040 Hz -> 3040 Hz (-29.2 dB)
harmonic 30: 52800 Hz -> 4800 Hz (-29.5 dB)
```

Harmonic 27 lands at **480 Hz**, below the note's own fundamental, only about 29 dB down. None of these are harmonics of 1760 Hz, so they sound like an inharmonic, metallic ring. As the note bends, they slide in the wrong directions. Low notes are less affected (their high harmonics are much weaker by the time they reach Nyquist), which is why naive oscillators can sound fine in the bass and terrible at the top.

> [!warning] You can't filter it out afterwards
> Once an alias is at 480 Hz, it's indistinguishable from a real 480 Hz component. A low-pass filter after the oscillator can't remove it without removing real content too. Aliasing has to be prevented where the high frequencies are *created*.

## Key takeaways

- Sawtooth and square jumps need slowly decaying harmonics, so high pitches alias strongly.
- A folded harmonic can fall below the fundamental and become an inharmonic tone.
- After folding, an alias cannot be distinguished from wanted content at the same frequency.

## Further reading

- [Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)
- [Aliasing — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliasing)
- [Sawtooth wave — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawtooth_wave)

lessons.title: Prevent aliasing before it folds
lessons.summary: Choose input filtering, band-limited oscillators and oversampling where new high frequencies are created.
lessons.body:
## Preventing aliasing in a synth

There are two situations.

**1. Sampling a real analogue signal (an ADC).** Here an **anti-aliasing filter** removes content above Nyquist *before* it can fold. Every audio interface input has one. In a modern delta-sigma ADC, the converter samples many times faster than the final sample rate, so a simple analogue low-pass in front is enough, and a steep digital filter does the rest before the rate is reduced to the final rate.

**2. Generating a signal digitally (an oscillator).** There's no analogue signal to filter: the samples are computed directly. So the oscillator itself must only generate content below Nyquist. Established techniques, at a conceptual level:

- **Additive synthesis:** sum sines for each harmonic, stopping below Nyquist. Exact, but costly for low notes with hundreds of harmonics.
- **Band-limited wavetables:** precompute a single cycle with only the harmonics that fit, keeping several tables for different pitch ranges and picking one per note.
- **BLIT:** construct a band-limited impulse train and integrate it to obtain the desired waveform, taking care with DC and numerical drift.
- **BLEP** methods: replace each naive discontinuity with a band-limited step, often by adding a precomputed correction. PolyBLEP uses a cheap polynomial approximation to the step correction.
- **Oversampling:** run the oscillator at, say, 4× the output rate, low-pass filter digitally, then discard samples. Aliases still occur, but further up where harmonics are weaker, and the filter removes content outside the output passband before downsampling. Aliases already folded into that passband remain.

The roadmap suggests comparing a naive waveform with a library's band-limited version rather than inventing a technique. Stilson and Smith's paper in the further reading is the classic overview.

**Nonlinear processing aliases too.** Clipping, distortion and waveshaping create new harmonics. FM creates sidebands, which need not be harmonics. A hard clipper applied to a 5 kHz sine creates harmonics at 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on, and those above Nyquist fold back. Oversampling around the nonlinear stage is the standard remedy.

## Key takeaways

- ADC input filtering removes unwanted high frequencies before sampling or decimation.
- Digital oscillators need band-limited generation or a suitable correction technique.
- Nonlinear processing also generates above-Nyquist content. Oversampling helps, but it does not make naive waveforms alias-free.

## Further reading

- [Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)
- [Oversampling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oversampling)
- [Hard Sync Without Aliasing — Eli Brandt](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~eli/papers/icmc01-hardsync.pdf)
