lessons.title: DAC images and reconstruction filters
lessons.summary: Distinguish out-of-band DAC images from in-band aliases and trace the conversion chain.
lessons.body:
## Reconstruction: the DAC side

A DAC is given one number per sample period. A crude converter holds each value until the next (a **zero-order hold**), producing a staircase. That staircase contains the wanted signal plus **image frequencies**: copies of the spectrum mirrored around multiples of the sample rate.

For a 1 kHz tone at a 48 kHz sample rate, the first images sit at 47 and 49 kHz: one kilohertz either side of the sample rate. More sit at 95 and 97 kHz, either side of twice the rate.

Images are not aliases. An alias is a folded component *inside* the represented band, created when sampling; images sit *above* Nyquist, created when converting back to analogue, and a filter can remove them.

A **reconstruction filter** (anti-imaging filter) removes the images, leaving the smooth wave the theorem promises. Most modern audio converters are **delta-sigma** designs that internally oversample and do much of this filtering digitally, so their external analogue filtering can be simple. Follow the converter or codec datasheet's recommended output circuit.

```flow
Analogue in
Anti-aliasing low-pass filter
ADC samples at the sample rate
Digital processing below Nyquist
DAC outputs samples
Reconstruction low-pass filter
Analogue out
```

## Key takeaways

- Holding samples creates image frequencies around multiples of the sample rate.
- Reconstruction filtering removes images; it cannot undo aliases already in the samples.
- Modern converters combine internal digital filtering with their specified analogue circuits.

## Further reading

- [Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sampling_Theorem.html)
- [Reconstruction filter — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_filter)
- [PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/pcm5102a.pdf)

options.explanation: Correct. Images appear either side of each multiple of the sample rate: 48 ± 1 kHz, 96 ± 1 kHz and so on. The zero-order hold attenuates them somewhat but doesn't remove them; the reconstruction filter does.

That is possible because they sit outside the wanted band; in-band aliases require prevention earlier.

lessons.title: Decibels and gain multipliers
lessons.summary: Choose amplitude or power decibels and convert a chain of gains to a sample multiplier.
lessons.body:
A synth that's too quiet is annoying. One that clips is broken: harsh, aliasing distortion every time a chord gets loud. Managing level is a constant job, from the first oscillator to the final converter, and decibels are the language for it.

## Why decibels

Level ratios in audio span an enormous range. An ideal signed 24-bit sample format has millions of steps between zero and full scale. Real converters have a higher analogue noise floor than that ideal resolution suggests. Ratios like that are unreadable as plain numbers, and our perception of loudness is roughly logarithmic anyway, so audio uses a logarithmic unit: the **decibel** (dB).

A decibel is always a **ratio** to something. There are two formulas, and mixing them up is the most common mistake. For quantities that measure power or energy:

```formula reference
L = 10 log_10(P_2 / P_1)
where
L: the level change, in decibels (dB); positive means louder
log_10: the base-10 logarithm, which answers "10 to what power gives this number?" (log_10(100) = 2)
P_1: the reference power (any unit, such as watts, W)
P_2: the power being compared, in the same unit as P_1; here twice P_1
dB: decibels, tenths of a bel
In words: ten times the logarithm of the power ratio gives decibels, so doubling the power is about +3 dB.
```

For amplitudes (sample values, voltages, sound pressures):

```formula reference
L = 20 log_10(A_2 / A_1)
where
L: the level change, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
A_1: the reference amplitude (a sample value, or volts, V)
A_2: the amplitude being compared, in the same unit; here twice A_1
dB: decibels
In words: twenty times the logarithm of the amplitude ratio gives decibels, so doubling an amplitude is about +6 dB.
```

Why the different factors? At unchanged impedance, power grows with squared voltage amplitude.

At the same impedance, doubling voltage quadruples power. The amplitude and power decibel rules therefore describe the same physical change when applied to the appropriate quantities.

Under that condition both formulas give the **same** dB value for the same change; you just use the one matching the quantity you have. Samples, voltages and pressures are **amplitudes**, so use the amplitude rule when comparing their magnitudes.

Going back from decibels to a multiplier undoes the logarithm:

```formula reference
g = 10^(L / 20)
where
g: the amplitude multiplier (gain factor) to apply to the samples; no unit
L: the level change, in decibels (dB); here −6 dB
10^x: 10 raised to the power x, the inverse of log_10
In words: divide the decibels by 20 and raise 10 to that power; −6 dB means multiply the samples by about 0.5.
```

Useful reference landmarks: **doubling an amplitude adds about 6 dB**, **×10 adds 20 dB**, and **×1.414 (the square root of 2) adds about 3 dB**. In power terms, doubling power is +3 dB. Gains in dB **add** where the ratios multiply:

A −6 dB stage followed by a −12 dB stage gives −18 dB overall, about one eighth of the original sample amplitude. Add the decibel changes; multiply the corresponding linear gains.

## Key takeaways

- Use twenty times the log for amplitude ratios and ten times the log for power ratios.
- Doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB; doubling power adds about 3 dB.
- Serial gains add in decibels and multiply as linear factors.

## Further reading

- [Decibel — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decibel)
- [Decibels and amplitude ratios — UNSW](https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/dB.html)

lessons.title: Peak, RMS and dBFS
lessons.summary: Measure digital level, compare crest factors and recognise different RMS meter conventions.
lessons.body:
## dBFS: decibels relative to full scale

**dBFS** measures a digital level relative to a defined full-scale reference. In a fixed PCM output format, that reference corresponds to the largest permitted sample level; floats can also hold values above it. With floats in ±1.0, full scale is 1.0, so the reference amplitude in the decibel formula is 1:

```formula reference
L = 20 log_10(|x| / 1.0)
where
L: the level, in decibels relative to full scale (dBFS)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
x: a sample value (or a peak value), with ±1.0 as full scale; here 0.5
|x|: the absolute value of x, its size ignoring the sign
dBFS: decibels relative to nominal full scale; 0 dBFS is the fixed-output reference, even though internal floats can exceed it
In words: compare a value with full scale (1.0) on the decibel scale; anything smaller than full scale gets a negative number.
```

0 dBFS is the nominal sample-peak maximum at a fixed-format output. Smaller peaks read negative: a peak of 0.5 is −6 dBFS, a peak of 0.1 is −20 dBFS. A value of 2.0 would be +6 dBFS: fine inside a float pipeline, but it will clip at the converter.

> [!note] RMS and dBFS conventions differ
> For **peak** levels, dBFS is unambiguous. For **RMS** levels, conventions differ. AES17 (and related IEC and ITU standards) defines the RMS of a full-scale *sine* as 0 dBFS, so a full-scale square wave reads +3 dBFS. Other meters use the plain maths, where a full-scale sine reads −3 dBFS RMS. When comparing figures, check which convention a meter or datasheet uses. This lesson uses the plain maths.

## Peak, RMS and crest factor

Two measurements describe a signal's level:

- **Peak level:** the largest absolute sample value. It decides whether the digital samples exceed the fixed-format limit. Reconstructed analogue peaks can be higher between samples, which needs a separate true-peak check.
- **RMS (root mean square):** the square root of the average of the squared samples. It tracks the signal's power, and relates more closely to perceived loudness than peak does.

The name describes the recipe, read from right to left: square every sample, take the mean, then the square root.

```formula reference
RMS = √((1 / N) × Σ x[n]^2)
where
RMS: root mean square, the signal's "average size" in the power sense, in the same units as the samples
N: the number of samples measured (ideally a whole number of cycles)
Σ: sigma, "add up": sum the following over every sample n from the first to the Nth
x[n]: sample number n
n: the sample index
√: square root
In words: square each sample (making them all positive), average the squares, and take the square root to get back to the samples' units.
```

For a steady sine measured over whole cycles, RMS is below peak.

For a sine measured over whole cycles, RMS is about 71% of its peak. A sine peaking at 0.5 therefore has RMS about 0.354. This is a waveform-specific relationship, not a rule for arbitrary audio.

The ratio of peak to RMS is the **crest factor**, often given in dB:

```formula reference
CF = A_pk / RMS
CF_dB = 20 log_10(A_pk / RMS)
where
CF: the crest factor, a plain ratio (no unit)
CF_dB: the crest factor in decibels (dB)
dB: decibels
A_pk: the peak value, the largest absolute sample
RMS: the root-mean-square value
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
In words: the crest factor says how spiky a signal is: how far its peaks stand above its average level. For a sine it is about 1.414, or 3 dB.
```

| Waveform | Crest factor | In dB |
|---|---|---|
| Square | 1 | 0 |
| Sine | 1.414 (square root of 2) | 3.01 |
| Saw, triangle | 1.732 (square root of 3) | 4.77 |
| Music (varies widely) | often much higher | 12–20 is an example |

A square wave and a sine with the same peak don't sound equally loud: the square has 3 dB more RMS. Switching from sine to square at the same peak increases RMS by 3 dB and often sounds louder, but perceived loudness also depends on spectrum and listening level. Synths may compensate per waveform.

## Key takeaways

- Peak level tells you whether nominal full scale is exceeded; RMS measures average squared signal size.
- Crest factor is peak divided by RMS: a sine has about 3 dB, a square has 0 dB.
- RMS dBFS references differ between meters. Check conventions before comparing figures.

## Further reading

- [dBFS — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBFS)
- [Crest factor — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_factor)

lessons.title: Summing voices and budgeting headroom
lessons.summary: Predict in-phase and unrelated sums and compare safe voice scaling with average-level scaling.
lessons.body:
## Summing signals

Mixing digital signals is just addition, sample by sample. What happens to the level depends on how the signals relate:

- **Identical, in phase:** amplitudes add. Two equal signals give +6.02 dB.
- **Identical, with opposite polarity:** they cancel.
- **Unrelated** (different frequencies, noise): **powers** add. Two equal signals give about +3 dB of RMS.

The distinction grows as more sources are added:

With unrelated equal-level voices, RMS grows more slowly than the worst-case peak: three voices add about 4.8 dB of RMS on average, whereas three identical aligned copies add about 9.5 dB. Average power does not bound the largest sample.

But peaks are what clip, and unrelated signals still line up their peaks now and then. Here's an A major triad, each voice a sine at 0.8 (−1.9 dBFS):

```python
import numpy as np

fs = 48_000
t = np.arange(fs) / fs
voices = [0.8*np.sin(2*np.pi*f*t)
          for f in (220, 277.18, 329.63)]
# Add corresponding samples of all voices.
mix = sum(voices)

def dbfs(v):
    return 20 * np.log10(v)

peak = np.max(np.abs(mix))
# Square, average, then take the root.
rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(mix**2))
for name, v in [("peak", peak),
                ("rms ", rms)]:
    print(f"{name} {v:.2f}",
          f"({dbfs(v):+.1f} dBFS)")
print("samples over 1.0:",
      np.sum(np.abs(mix) > 1.0))
```

```text
peak 2.40 (+7.6 dBFS)
rms  0.98 (-0.2 dBFS)
samples over 1.0: 15337
```

The RMS rose by the expected amount for three unrelated signals:

One of these voices has RMS about 0.566. Three together have RMS about 0.98, as expected for unrelated equal-level signals over this capture.

But the three peaks nearly align, reaching about 2.4. Converted to a fixed format, almost a third of the samples would clip.

**Headroom** is the gap between your normal peak level and 0 dBFS. Two common policies scale each voice by the voice count or its square root. They serve different goals.

- Assuming each voice is bounded by full scale, dividing each by the maximum voice count bounds the mathematical sum at full scale, but makes single notes quiet.
- Dividing by the square root of the voice count keeps average RMS steadier for unrelated voices but can still peak over. Many designs do this and add a soft clipper or limiter at the end to catch the rare peaks.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Several taps feeding one drain
> A drain can carry the flow from any one tap, yet simultaneous surges from several taps can exceed its flow capacity. Average flow alone does not describe a brief surge.
>
> **How it maps:** Tap flow rates are simultaneous voice sample values, and drain flow capacity is the output range. The sample values add, so aligned peaks can exceed that range even when individual voices and average RMS look modest.
>
> **Where it stops:** Audio values can be positive or negative and can cancel; water flow in this picture cannot. RMS power addition also follows signal statistics, rather than adding average tap flows directly.

## Key takeaways

- Identical in-phase signals add amplitudes; unrelated signals add power on average.
- Unrelated signals can still align their peaks and exceed full scale.
- Dividing by voice count protects against the worst case; square-root scaling needs protection for overshoots.

## Further reading

- [Decibel — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decibel)
- [dBFS — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBFS)
- [Gain stage — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gain_stage)
- [Decibels and signal combination — UNSW](https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/dB.html)

lessons.title: Hard and soft clipping harmonics
lessons.summary: Compare clipping curves and measure the new harmonics that require alias control.
lessons.body:
## Clipping: hard and soft

When a signal exceeds what a stage can represent, it **clips**.

**Hard clipping** flattens anything beyond the limit:

Values within minus one to plus one pass unchanged; values beyond either endpoint are held at that limit. For example, an input of 1.7 becomes 1.0.

Explicit saturating conversion does this. A raw integer cast is not a clipper: out-of-range conversion can wrap or be undefined, so clamp before converting to the DAC format. It creates a sharp corner where the wave meets the ceiling, and sharp corners mean strong high harmonics. A symmetric clip of a sine, or another input with half-wave symmetry, creates only odd harmonics before sampling. Symmetry of the clipper alone does not remove even harmonics already in an arbitrary input.

**Soft clipping** bends the wave gradually towards the limit. A common choice is the hyperbolic tangent:

The `tanh` function is almost straight near zero and flattens towards minus one and plus one. It changes 0.1 only slightly, to about 0.0997, but compresses 2.0 to about 0.964.

Small signals pass almost unchanged; big ones are squashed smoothly. It still distorts, but its high harmonics fall away much faster.

Compare both on a 1 kHz sine driven 6 dB over full scale (amplitude 2.0). The levels are relative to the fundamental:

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f = 768_000, 1_000   # see note below
t = np.arange(fs) / fs
x = 2.0 * np.sin(2*np.pi*f*t)

# Flatten overshoots; tanh bends them.
hard = np.clip(x, -1.0, 1.0)
soft = np.tanh(x)

def harmonic_db(y, k):
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y))
    # Here 1 Hz bins match integer hertz.
    return 20*np.log10(spec[k*f] / spec[f])

for k in (3, 5, 7, 9):
    h = harmonic_db(hard, k)
    s = harmonic_db(soft, k)
    print(f"H{k}: hard {h:6.1f}",
          f" soft {s:6.1f} dB")
```

```text
H3: hard  -12.9  soft  -15.5 dB
H5: hard  -26.9  soft  -28.3 dB
H7: hard  -35.8  soft  -40.9 dB
H9: hard  -32.9  soft  -53.4 dB
```

(The FFT reading is explained in the FFT measurement units. This experiment runs at a very high sample rate to greatly reduce alias contamination of the harmonics measured here. A finite sample rate cannot eliminate every alias from ideal hard clipping.)

By the 9th harmonic, soft clipping is about 20 dB cleaner. Inside a synth running at 48 kHz, both clippers' harmonics above 24 kHz will **alias**, which is why distortion stages are often oversampled.

> [!tip] Clipping as a sound
> Deliberate saturation is a classic synth effect. Accidental clipping at the output is a fault. The difference is whether you chose where it happens and controlled its aliasing.

## Key takeaways

- Hard clipping flattens over-range samples; a raw integer cast is not a safe clipper.
- Soft clipping bends smoothly and usually produces weaker high harmonics for comparable drive.
- Both introduce nonlinear harmonics; control aliasing around intentional distortion stages.

## Further reading

- [Clipping (audio) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipping_(audio))

lessons.title: Stage gain and protect the output
lessons.summary: Place headroom and protection in a float synth and measure worst-case patches.
lessons.body:
## Gain staging inside a digital synth

**Gain staging** means setting the level at each stage so that no stage clips and none is needlessly quiet. Floating-point storage allows intermediate values above nominal full scale, but effects may deliberately limit or saturate them. A typical output path is:

```flow
Oscillators, each about -6 to -12 dBFS
Voice mixer: scale for the number of sources
Filter: resonance can boost near cutoff
Amp envelope and velocity
Voice sum: scale for polyphony
Effects: check for level build-up
Master gain, then soft clip or limiter
Convert to the codec format (hard limit)
```

Practical rules:

1. **Know where the hard limit is.** The final fixed-format conversion needs a bound. Intermediate floats can exceed 1.0, but check each effect for its own saturation or input limits.
2. **Budget headroom where levels can grow:** summing voices, resonant filters (which can boost signals near the cutoff well above the input level) and feedback effects.
3. **Protect the output.** A soft clipper or limiter just before conversion turns rare overshoots into mild saturation instead of harsh clipping.
4. **Measure.** Log peak and RMS in an offline render of your worst case: all voices, full resonance, maximum velocity.
5. **Change gain smoothly.** Jumping a gain value between samples can cause clicks; stepping it in coarse increments when a knob turns causes "zipper noise". Smoothing is covered in the synthesis module.

## Key takeaways

- Budget headroom for mixing, resonance and feedback effects.
- Intermediate float signals can exceed nominal full scale; protect the final fixed-format conversion.
- Measure worst-case peak and RMS, and smooth control changes to avoid clicks and zipper noise.

## Further reading

- [dBFS — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBFS)
- [Gain stage — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gain_stage)

lessons.title: From digital full scale to line voltage
lessons.summary: Convert dBu and dBV to RMS volts and match the synth output to its destination safely.
lessons.body:
## From dBFS to volts

The DAC turns 0 dBFS into some maximum output voltage. That voltage is set by the codec and the output circuit, so it's on the board's datasheet, not a universal number. What your audio interface expects is in its manual. Two common nominal **line levels** use different references:

| Level | Reference | RMS voltage |
|---|---|---|
| +4 dBu (pro) | 0 dBu = 0.7746 V | ≈ 1.228 V |
| −10 dBV (consumer) | 0 dBV = 1 V | ≈ 0.316 V |

Converting either unit to an RMS voltage is the decibel formula run backwards, with that unit's reference voltage:

```formula reference
V = V_ref × 10^(L / 20)
where
V: the RMS voltage, in volts (V)
V_ref: the reference voltage: 0.7746 V for dBu, 1 V for dBV
L: the level, in dBu or dBV; here +4 dBu and −10 dBV
10^x: 10 raised to the power x
dBu: decibels relative to 0.7746 V RMS
dBV: decibels relative to 1 V RMS
In words: +4 dBu is 4 dB above 0.7746 V, about 1.228 V RMS; −10 dBV is 10 dB below 1 V, about 0.316 V RMS.
```

These are *nominal* levels; real signals peak well above them, and equipment has headroom for that. Check both the synth's maximum output and the interface input's maximum level in their manuals, and set the synth's output level so that its loudest patch doesn't overload the input.

> [!warning] Keep to line-level connections
> Turn the monitor level down before testing a new connection and raise it gradually. Line, instrument, microphone, headphone and speaker connections are not interchangeable. Never connect a power amplifier's speaker output to a line input or to a development board. Work only with low-voltage, battery or USB-powered circuits and the board's documented audio outputs, and add any output protection the board's documentation recommends.

## Key takeaways

- dBu and dBV use different RMS voltage references; digital dBFS depends on the actual converter and circuit.
- Nominal line level leaves headroom for signal peaks. Check both devices’ maximum levels.

lessons.title: Check and plot an offline test signal
lessons.summary: Build a reproducible Python workbench and check signal length, level, DC and zero-crossing frequency.
lessons.body:
Ears are good at telling you *something* is wrong and bad at telling you *what*. Is that buzz aliasing or clipping? Is the note 3 cents flat, or is it a filter making it sound duller? The roadmap's readiness test for this stage is to "explain each sample's meaning, verify frequency and level from the data". This lesson builds a small offline toolkit for doing exactly that.

The tools are standard: **numpy** for arrays and the FFT, **matplotlib** for plots, **soundfile** for WAV files. You're *using* an FFT, not writing one; FFT implementation is deliberately deferred.

## Set up

Use a virtual environment so the experiments are reproducible from a clean checkout:

```text
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install numpy matplotlib soundfile
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Commit `requirements.txt` with your experiments. The outputs below were produced with numpy 2.5, matplotlib 3.11 and soundfile 0.14; numbers in the last decimal place may differ slightly on other versions.

> [!warning] Protect your ears and speakers
> A full-scale sine is very loud and fatiguing. Generate test files at −12 dBFS or lower, turn the monitor level down before playing anything new, and raise it gradually. Never play untested generated audio on headphones at volume.

## Generate a test signal and check it numerically

Start with a known signal and check that the numbers match the theory:

```python
import numpy as np

fs = 48_000

def tone(f, secs=1.0, amp=0.5, fs=fs):
    n = np.arange(int(secs * fs))
    # Sample index divided by rate is time.
    return amp * np.sin(2*np.pi*f*n/fs)

x = tone(997)
print(len(x), x.dtype)
print(f"peak {np.max(np.abs(x)):.4f}")
rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2))
print(f"rms  {rms:.4f}")
# A whole-cycle sine should have no DC.
print("dc ok:", abs(np.mean(x)) < 1e-9)
```

```text
48000 float64
peak 0.5000
rms  0.3536
dc ok: True
```

Each check has a reason:

- **Length:** 1 s at 48 kHz must be 48,000 samples. Off-by-one-block errors show up here.
- **Peak** 0.5 is −6.02 dBFS, as requested.
- **RMS** 0.3536 is the peak divided by 1.414 (the square root of 2), the sine's crest factor (the peak-and-RMS unit).
- **DC offset** (the mean) should be essentially zero for this whole-cycle capture. Partial cycles can have a non-zero mean even when the underlying wave is centred correctly. A persistent offset over complete cycles means the waveform is shifted off centre, which wastes headroom and can thump when audio starts and stops.

Other cheap sanity checks are worth wrapping in a function: `np.isfinite(x).all()` (NaN or infinity anywhere means a bug, often a filter blowing up), and the number of samples at or beyond ±1.0.

## Plot the waveform

A plot shows what summary numbers hide: discontinuities, glitches at block boundaries, asymmetry.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")      # no window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(480)             # 10 ms
x = 0.5 * np.sin(2*np.pi*440*n/fs)

# Plot sample times in milliseconds.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(n / fs * 1000, x, marker=".",
        linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)
ax.grid(True)
fig.savefig("sine.png", dpi=120)
print("saved sine.png")
```

```text
saved sine.png
```

Plot **short windows** (a few cycles) to see the shape, and mark the samples as dots, because they're the real data. The lines joining them are just a drawing aid; recall from the reconstruction unit that the true reconstructed signal is smooth, not straight-sided. Fixing the y-axis at ±1 makes levels comparable between plots.

## Measure frequency in the time domain

For a clean, single-frequency signal, count **upward zero crossings**: places where a sample is negative and the next one isn't. Average the spacing between them:

```python
import numpy as np
fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(fs)
x = 0.5 * np.sin(2*np.pi*997*n/fs)

# upward zero crossings: - to + sign change
s = np.signbit(x)
# Select negative-to-nonnegative crossings.
ups = np.flatnonzero(s[:-1] & ~s[1:])
# Crossing gaps become seconds per cycle.
periods = np.diff(ups) / fs
print(f"{1 / np.mean(periods):.2f} Hz")
```

```text
997.01 Hz
```

The frequency is one over the average period, where each period is measured in samples and converted to seconds.

Average the gaps between upward crossings to estimate one cycle’s length. More samples between crossings mean a lower frequency; a higher sample rate makes the same sample gap represent less time.

This counts whole samples, so it's only accurate to a fraction of a sample per period (here 0.01 Hz after averaging many periods). It's fooled by noise and by waveforms with several crossings per cycle. For anything richer than a sine, use the spectrum.

## Key takeaways

- Check sample count, peak, RMS, DC offset and finiteness before listening at a safe level.
- Plot short windows with sample dots; joining lines are a visual aid.
- Upward zero crossings estimate a clean sine’s period but are unreliable on noisy or complex waveforms.

## Further reading

- [numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [python-soundfile documentation](https://python-soundfile.readthedocs.io/)

lessons.title: FFT bins and capture length
lessons.summary: Read FFT frequency axes and choose enough observation time to distinguish nearby tones.
lessons.body:
## Read a spectrum with numpy's FFT

The **FFT** (fast Fourier transform) takes a finite capture of samples and returns how much of each frequency they contain, at evenly spaced frequencies called **FFT bins**. For real input (ordinary audio), the negative-frequency spectrum mirrors the positive half in magnitude. NumPy's `rfft` therefore returns only the non-negative bins. For even input lengths these include the Nyquist frequency; for odd lengths the last bin lies just below it. Use `np.fft.rfftfreq` with the same capture length and actual sample spacing to generate the matching frequency axis:


```formula reference
K = N / 2 + 1
Δf = fs / N
f_k = k × Δf
where
K: the number of bins rfft returns (when N is even)
N: the number of samples analysed (the capture length)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second
Δf: delta f, the bin spacing: the frequency gap between neighbouring bins, in hertz (Hz)
f_k: the frequency at the centre of bin number k, in hertz (Hz)
k: the bin index, 0, 1, 2, … up to N/2; bin 0 is 0 Hz (DC) and bin N/2 is the Nyquist frequency
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: A longer capture gives closer FFT bins: one second gives one-hertz spacing. For even-length real input, the result includes both zero frequency and Nyquist, giving half the input length plus one bins.
```

Three facts you need to read it correctly:

1. **Bin spacing** is the sample rate divided by the number of samples. One second at 48 kHz gives 1 Hz bins; 0.1 s gives 10 Hz bins. Longer captures give finer frequency resolution.
2. **Scaling:** NumPy’s raw output grows with the number of input samples. For ordinary positive-frequency bins, multiply by 2 and divide by the sum of the window (in the next unit). DC and the even-length Nyquist bin have no negative-frequency partner and are not doubled.
3. **Windowing:** multiply the capture by a smooth **window** (Hann is a good default) that tapers its ends to zero. Without it, a frequency that doesn't fit a whole number of cycles in the capture smears energy across the spectrum. That smearing is called **spectral leakage**.

Zero-padding a capture gives more displayed frequency points by interpolating the same transform. It adds no measured information and cannot replace a longer capture when separating nearby tones.

## Key takeaways

- For even-length real input, rfft returns half the sample count plus one bins.
- Bin spacing is sample rate divided by capture length in samples.
- Longer captures give finer bin spacing; windowing and correct scaling are also needed to read a spectrum.

## Further reading

- [numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfftfreq.html)
- [Zero padding and spectral interpolation — Julius O. Smith](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/sasp/Zero_Padding_Time_Domain.html)

lessons.title: Window and scale FFT amplitudes
lessons.summary: Use a Hann window and the window sum to recover a bin-centred sine’s amplitude.
lessons.body:
Analyse a real sample array with NumPy's `rfft`. In this unit, the capture length is the number of input samples and bins are indexed from zero. A bin-centred sine completes a whole number of cycles in the capture.

## Window and scale an FFT

The Hann window NumPy uses is a smooth raised-cosine taper.

The window tapers the capture towards zero at both ends, reducing the artificial jump caused by analysing a finite segment. For an even-length Hann window, the centre gets just below one rather than exactly one.

Windowing also reduces the measured magnitude. To recover a bin-centred sine’s amplitude, account for the actual window sum. Ordinary positive-frequency bins need doubling because the real sine has a mirrored negative-frequency contribution:

```formula reference
A = 2 × |X[k]| / Σ w[n]
where
A: the amplitude of a sine whose frequency sits on bin k
X[k]: the raw complex FFT output for bin k
|X[k]|: its magnitude (size), which numpy gives with np.abs
k: the bin index
Σ w[n]: sigma means add all the window values: the sample count without a taper, and about half that count for Hann
w[n]: the window value for sample n
n: the sample index
In words: To measure a bin-centred sine, divide its FFT magnitude by the sum of the window and double ordinary positive-frequency bins. Do not double zero frequency or the even-length Nyquist bin.
```

The 0 Hz bin and, for even capture lengths, the Nyquist bin have no separate mirror, so they are not doubled; the `spectrum` function below halves them back.

```python
import numpy as np

def spectrum(x, fs):
    w = np.hanning(len(x))
    # Taper the ends before the transform.
    X = np.fft.rfft(x * w)
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)
    # scale so a sine of amplitude A reads A
    # Correct the window’s amplitude loss.
    mag = np.abs(X) * 2 / np.sum(w)
    mag[0] *= 0.5  # DC has no mirror
    if len(x) % 2 == 0:
        mag[-1] *= 0.5  # Nyquist too
    return freqs, mag

fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(fs)
x = 0.5 * np.sin(2*np.pi*997*n/fs)
freqs, mag = spectrum(x, fs)
# Locate the strongest frequency bin.
k = np.argmax(mag)
print(f"bin width {freqs[1]:.1f} Hz")
print(f"peak at {freqs[k]:.1f} Hz,"
      f" {20*np.log10(mag[k]):.2f} dBFS")
```

```text
bin width 1.0 Hz
peak at 997.0 Hz, -6.02 dBFS
```

Both the frequency and the level match what we generated: the round trip from theory to data and back works.

## Key takeaways

- A Hann window tapers the capture endpoints to reduce abrupt boundaries.
- Divide FFT magnitude by the window sum and double ordinary positive-frequency bins.
- DC and the even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled; accurate bin-level readings assume a bin-centred tone.

## Further reading

- [numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfftfreq.html)
- [Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectrum_Analysis_Windows.html)
- [numpy.hanning — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.hanning.html)

lessons.title: Leakage and tones between bins
lessons.summary: Compare rectangular and Hann captures and explain why between-bin peak readings understate amplitude.
lessons.body:
FFT bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the capture length in samples. The preceding FFT units explain the amplitude scaling; here we compare what happens when a tone falls between bins.

## Leakage between FFT bins

What if the frequency falls *between* bins? With a 0.1 s capture (10 Hz bins), compare 1000 Hz (exactly on a bin) with 1005 Hz (halfway between two bins), with and without a window:

```python
import numpy as np
fs, N = 48_000, 4_800          # 0.1 s
n = np.arange(N)
wins = {"rect": np.ones(N),
        "hann": np.hanning(N)}
for f in (1000.0, 1005.0):
    x = 0.5 * np.sin(2*np.pi*f*n/fs)
    for name, w in wins.items():
        mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x*w))
        # Compare amplitudes on one scale.
        mag = mag * 2 / np.sum(w)
        db = 20*np.log10(mag + 1e-12)
        # Floor tiny magnitudes at -120 dB.
        db = np.maximum(db, -120)
        pk = db.max()
        far = db[150]        # 1.5 kHz
        print(f"{f:.0f} {name}:",
              f"peak {pk:6.2f},",
              f"1.5k {far:6.1f}")
```

```text
1000 rect: peak  -6.02, 1.5k -120.0
1000 hann: peak  -6.02, 1.5k -120.0
1005 rect: peak  -9.92, 1.5k  -51.8
1005 hann: peak  -7.44, 1.5k -117.7
```

(−120 here means "at or below −120 dB"; the floor hides meaningless rounding noise.)

- On this bin, both recover the expected level to the displayed precision.
- Between bins, the **unwindowed** ("rect") capture loses 3.9 dB at the peak and leaks energy to −52 dB as far as 500 Hz away, which would mask real low-level components such as aliases.
- The **Hann** window loses only 1.4 dB at the peak and keeps the far leakage near −118 dB.

A between-bin amplitude shortfall is called **scalloping loss**. For accurate amplitudes, use coherent sampling (whole cycles), a flat-top window (which widens the main peak), or a peak-interpolation method with an amplitude correction matched to the chosen window.

Practical consequences: window when leakage is a concern; a rectangular window is suitable for a coherent capture containing whole cycles. Read levels from a capture long enough that the bins are fine; and when you need an exact level, generate test frequencies that land on bins (an integer number of cycles in the capture).

## Key takeaways

- An unwindowed, between-bin tone leaks energy into distant bins and can hide faint components.
- A Hann window reduces distant leakage, but a between-bin peak still underreads amplitude.
- For an exact level check, capture a whole number of cycles and use the correct scaling.

## Further reading

- [Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectrum_Analysis_Windows.html)
- [Window function — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Window_function)
- [Spectral leakage — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_leakage)
- [Flat-top amplitude measurement — SciPy documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.windows.flattop.html)

A longer capture alone does not guarantee better alignment.

lessons.title: Measure predicted waveform aliases
lessons.summary: Compare a naive sawtooth’s spectrum with predicted folded harmonics and recognise aliases hidden on harmonic bins.
lessons.body:
## Verify an aliasing prediction

The sharp-waveform unit predicted where a naive 1,760 Hz sawtooth's harmonics fold at 48 kHz. Now measure it. A 1 s capture makes each bin exactly 1 Hz, so bin index equals frequency:

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f0 = 48_000, 1_760
n = np.arange(fs)                  # 1 s
phase = (f0 * n / fs) % 1.0
saw = 2 * phase - 1                # naive

w = np.hanning(fs)
X = np.fft.rfft(saw * w)
mag = np.abs(X) * 2 / w.sum()
db = 20 * np.log10(mag + 1e-12)
ref = db[f0]               # fundamental

for hz in (480, 1280, 2240, 3040, 3520):
    real = hz % f0 == 0
    kind = "harmonic" if real else "alias"
    # Level relative to the fundamental.
    rel = db[hz] - ref
    print(f"{hz:>5} Hz {rel:6.1f} dB",
          kind)
```

```text
  480 Hz  -28.5 dB alias
 1280 Hz  -28.8 dB alias
 2240 Hz  -28.2 dB alias
 3040 Hz  -29.1 dB alias
 3520 Hz   -6.0 dB harmonic
```

The predictions were −28.6, −28.9, −28.3 and −29.2 dB for the four aliases (each harmonic's amplitude is one over its harmonic number, here 27, 28, 26 and 29), and −6.0 dB for the 2nd harmonic. The measurements agree to about 0.1 dB, and the small differences come from other, much weaker harmonics folding onto the same bins. This is the "compare a deliberately aliased signal with its predicted apparent frequency" exercise from the roadmap. Later, run the same script against a band-limited oscillator from a library and watch those aliases drop.

If the sample rate is an exact multiple of a waveform’s fundamental, aliases can land on existing harmonic bins. They then change harmonic levels rather than appear as extra inharmonic lines. Test awkward frequencies as well as neat ones.

## Key takeaways

- Predict alias frequencies and relative levels before measuring the spectrum.
- Several higher harmonics can fold onto the same bin, changing its observed level.
- A neat ratio of note frequency to sample rate can hide aliases on existing harmonics; also test awkward frequencies.

## Further reading

- [numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectrum_Analysis_Windows.html)

questions.prompt: You analyse a naive 3,000 Hz square wave generated at 48 kHz. The spectrum shows components only at 3, 9, 15 and 21 kHz: no inharmonic aliases at all. But the 21 kHz component reads −14.0 dB relative to the fundamental, while an ideal square's 7th harmonic has 1/7 of the fundamental's amplitude, about −16.9 dB. What is going on?

options.text: The 48 kHz sample rate is an exact multiple of the 3 kHz note (48,000 = 16 × 3,000), so every alias folds onto an existing harmonic. Aliasing is present but hidden: it changes the harmonic levels instead of adding inharmonic tones
options.explanation: Correct. For example, the 9th harmonic (27 kHz) folds to 21 kHz and the 11th (33 kHz) to 15 kHz, so their energy piles onto harmonic bins. Detune the oscillator slightly and inharmonic aliases appear.

options.text: There's no aliasing; the 21 kHz reading is just FFT error
options.explanation: The FFT on exact bins is accurate. The 2.9 dB discrepancy is real.

options.text: Square waves never alias because they only have odd harmonics
options.explanation: Odd harmonics above Nyquist still fold. Only their landing places are special here.

options.text: The −14.0 dB means the sample rate is too high
options.explanation: A higher sample rate would *reduce* aliasing and bring the 21 kHz level closer to −16.9 dB.

questions.workedExample:
1. Odd harmonics: 3, 9, 15, 21, 27, 33, 39, 45, … kHz.
2. Fold at a 48 kHz sample rate: 27 → 21, 33 → 15, 39 → 9, 45 → 3, and so on.
3. Because 48 kHz is exactly 16 × 3 kHz, every fold lands on 3, 9, 15 or 21 kHz.
4. Those bins now hold the true harmonic plus folded energy, so the levels are wrong (21 kHz reads −14.0 dB instead of −16.9 dB).

Testing at a 'neat' frequency can hide aliasing. Test oscillators at awkward frequencies (like 997 Hz or a detuned note) where aliases land between harmonics.

lessons.title: Write WAV files and check the round trip
lessons.summary: Export with explicit clipping and fades, then verify rate, subtype, length and quantisation error.
lessons.body:
## Write a WAV file with a library

Writing a WAV encoder isn't a learning goal; a library handles the format. `soundfile` (a wrapper for libsndfile) takes float arrays and converts them to the requested **subtype**:

```python
import numpy as np
import soundfile as sf

fs = 48_000
n = np.arange(2 * fs)                # 2 s
# -12 dBFS sine
x = 0.25 * np.sin(2*np.pi*440*n/fs)

# 10 ms fades so the file doesn't click
ramp = np.linspace(0, 1, fs // 100)
x[:ramp.size] *= ramp
# Reverse the ramp for a smooth ending.
x[-ramp.size:] *= ramp[::-1]

x = np.clip(x, -1.0, 1.0)    # be explicit
sf.write("a440.wav", x, fs,
         subtype="PCM_24")

# Read back to check the stored result.
y, fs2 = sf.read("a440.wav")
info = sf.info("a440.wav")
print(fs2, info.subtype, len(y))
# Largest sample difference after export.
err = np.max(np.abs(y - x))
print(f"max error {err:.1e}")
```

```text
48000 PCM_24 96000
max error 1.2e-07
```

Reading the file back and comparing is the important habit. The sample rate, format and length are as intended, and the error is at most one 24-bit step (2⁻²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁷). That's quantisation, not a bug. It's a full step rather than the half step that rounding would give because, in the libsndfile version bundled here (1.2.2), the clipping conversion rounds *down*: every error lies between 0 and −1 step. At 24 bits that's harmless, but it's exactly the kind of detail a read-back check reveals.

Notes:

- `sf.read` returns float64 by default; integer PCM files are scaled around ±1.0. Float-format files can contain values outside that range. Pass an integer type, as in `sf.read(path, dtype="int16")` (or `"int32"`), to get integers instead. These are scaled to fill the integer type, not the file's raw values: a 16-bit file read as int16 gives its stored samples, but a 24-bit file read as int32 comes back multiplied by 256.
- Use `sf.write(path, x, fs, subtype="FLOAT")` to keep a 32-bit float file with headroom above 1.0 for analysis. Use `PCM_16` or `PCM_24` for files to share or import into a DAW.
- `soundfile` switches on libsndfile's clipping option whenever it opens a file, so in testing it clipped 1.7 to full scale when writing PCM rather than wrapping it. **Clip explicitly** anyway, so your output never depends on a library setting.
- The fades matter: a file that starts or ends mid-wave clicks, which is easy to mistake for a synth bug.

## A measurement checklist

Before trusting any experiment's audio, check:

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| Length and rate | `len(x)`, `sf.info` |
| Finite values | `np.isfinite(x).all()` |
| Peak level | `np.max(np.abs(x))`, then dBFS |
| RMS and DC | `np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2))`, `np.mean(x)` |
| Full-scale warnings | `np.sum(np.abs(x) >= 1)` |
| Frequency | windowed FFT peak |
| Unwanted content | FFT, compare with prediction |

Then listen at a safe level. Measurement tells you what's there; listening tells you whether it matters.

## Key takeaways

- Use the library’s subtype to choose PCM or float storage and clip explicitly before PCM output.
- Short fades prevent start and stop discontinuities.
- Read each file back to check metadata and sample error; library versions can affect conversion details.

## Further reading

- [python-soundfile documentation](https://python-soundfile.readthedocs.io/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about writing and reading WAV files with `soundfile` are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: For a 16-bit file, `sf.read(path, dtype='int16')` returns the stored integers rather than values scaled to ±1.0
options.explanation: Correct. Integer dtypes return integers scaled to fill that type, so a 16-bit file read as int16 gives its stored samples. (A 24-bit file read as int32 comes back multiplied by 256.) The default float64 read is scaled to ±1.0.

options.text: Writing with `sf.write(path, x, fs, subtype='FLOAT')` can preserve values above 1.0 for later analysis
options.explanation: Correct. A FLOAT file preserves headroom above nominal full scale, with float32 precision. Converting from float64 may round; PCM subtypes cannot preserve samples beyond their full-scale range.

options.text: You should clip to ±1.0 yourself before writing PCM, rather than relying on library behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. soundfile happens to switch on libsndfile's clipping option, but making it explicit means your output never depends on a library setting.

options.text: Short fades at the start and end prevent clicks that could be mistaken for synth bugs
options.explanation: Correct. Starting or stopping mid-cycle creates a step, which clicks.

options.text: You must write your own WAV encoder to control the bit depth
options.explanation: The `subtype` argument (PCM_16, PCM_24, FLOAT …) controls the format. Writing an encoder isn't needed.

1. 16-bit file read as int16 → stored values, not ±1.0 floats. ✓
2. FLOAT subtype keeps over-range values. ✓
3. Explicit clipping → behaviour you control. ✓
4. Fades → no start/stop discontinuity. ✓
5. subtype handles bit depth. ✗

And always read the file back to check rate, subtype, length and the round-trip error, as the lesson did (at most one 24-bit step).
